Preface
 
This book covers the Cucumber BDD test automation tool. BDD stands for Behavior driven development. BDD is an extension of TDD that makes use of a simple, Domain Specific Language (DSL). The DSL is in plain English and converts natural language statements into executable tests. The DSL that we are going to study in this book is known by the name Gherkin. The term Gherkin however is specific to Cucumber, JBehave, Behave and Behat software tools.
 
This book will be divided into three sections:
 
Section 1 will explore what Cucumber is along with the building blocks such as Feature files, Step Definition classes and Runner classes. These will form the foundation for getting up-to-speed with Cucumber.
 
Section 2 will explore the Page Object design pattern and make the reader understand Page Objects and Page Factories.
 
Section 3 will explore the integration part of Cucumber with TestNG and Maven. We will be putting the Maven build in Jenkins and thus configure Jenkins for automatic triggering on completion of a Dev build.
 
After reading this book, the test engineer will be conversant with incorporating Cucumber as a BDD framework in his testing and thus streamlining the testing and bug detection process.
 
Section I
 
Chapter 1 makes you understand the concept of Test Driven Development(TDD) followed by Behavior Driven Development(BDD).TDD stands for Test Driven Development.
 
Chapter describes the Feature files which are the documents that contain Gherkin scenarios and requirements – they can be very useful to teams working on BDD. Feature file is a key deliverable for BAs. Feature files are where BAs store the requirements in Gherkin format and create the bridge between requirements and automated tests.
 
Chapter 3 describes about the Gherkin statements which are present in the Feature files and are translated into code using what is called a Step Definition. It is the bridge between the utility Java classes which will be the Page Objects and the Feature files. The Step Definition files contain regular expressions in addition to Java code.
 
Chapter 4 will cover the test runner class which also acts as an interlink between feature files and step definition classes. It is in the test runner class, that you provide the path for both feature file and step definition class.
 
Section II
 
Chapter 5 onwards, we will jump into action by first understanding the Page Object Design Pattern and Page Object Model. We will the create Page Objects for all the individual Web Pages in the Application Under Test[AUT]. A page object contains logic for working with all HTML objects on the Page.
 
Chapter 6 will cover the PageFactory Class in Selenium which is an extension to the Page Object design pattern. It is used to initialize the elements of the Page Object or instantiate the Page Objects itself. It is used to initialize elements of a Page class without having to use 'FindElement' or 'FindElements'. We will create Page factories fr static web elements.
 
Section III
 
Chapter 7 will cover TestNG in Selenium which is a testing framework in Java, inspired by JUnit and NUnit. It overcomes the constraints of JUnit. From simple unit testing to complex integrated testing, it simplifies all testing requirements such as functional testing, regression, end-to-end testing and more. We will create a TestNG xml file and configure our tests.
 
Chapter 8 will cover Apache Maven, which is a software project management and comprehension tool. Based on the concept of a project object model (POM), Maven can manage a project's build, reporting and documentation from a central piece of information.
 
Chapter 9 will show us one can execute a Maven Project from Eclipse IDE and later externalize the execution process from command line. This is required because we will be integrating the Maven build in Jenkins.
 
Chapter 10 will cover the configuration of POM.xml to execute the TestNG xml which will eventually run our Cucumber tests. The POM.xml will be the single execution engine for our framework. We will see how to execute the TestNG xml from Maven's POM.xml.
 
Chapter 11 will be configuring the Cucumber Reporter in the runner class and generate reports with statistics for our framework.
 
Chapter 12 will show how we can configure graphical extent reports for our project using Extent Reports, which gives more insight on the test execution status.
 
Chapter 13 will cover the execution of Cucumber features parallelly using TestNG XML and the ThreadLocal class of Java. Parallel execution speeds up the overall test execution thus reducing time for test completion
 
Chapter 14 will first cover Jenkins and then we will be integrating the framework with Jenkins and doing configurations for auto trigger.

CHAPTER 1
 
Introduction to Behavior Driven Development
 
Welcome to the exciting world of Behavior Driven Development ( BDD ). This book will be divided into three parts. The first part will make the user understand what Cucumber is all about. The second part will explore the Page Object Model and Page Factories. The third part will cover integration of Cucumber with the TestNG framework. It is going to be a very exciting journey, so let’s get started and understand what BDD is all about.
 
BDD helps to bridge the gap between business people and technical people by implementing a language called It consists of statements in English predominantly, although other languages are available for this purpose too. A group of Gherkin statements together lists a functional flow. These statements are taken by the Automation developer and converted into code using frameworks like Cucumber, JBehave or Specflow. BDD is quite frequently used in Agile projects for getting quick feedback on code quality after developers check in their code in source code management systems like GitHub or SVN. The BDD tests can be configured to execute immediately after the code is checked in.
 
This chapter will predominantly focus on
  
Test Driven Development
 
Behavior Driven Development
 
Understanding Gherkin
 
Introduction to Cucumber
 
Understanding the DRY principle
 
Components of Cucumber
 
Setup of the project in Eclipse
 
Setup of TestNG in Eclipse
 
Understanding the project structure

 
Objective
 
After reading this chapter, the reader will be conversant with the concepts of TDD, BDD, Gherkin and able to create a basic file called in the Gherkin Language. He will also learn how the Gherkin file relates to the Step Definition file which is one of the components of Cucumber. He will get knowledge of the project structure and understand how to set up a project in Eclipse along with TestNG Plugin integration. This chapter will serve as the foundation for one who wishes to work as a Test Automation Engineer and wants to make a career in BDD framework.

 
1.1 What is TDD?
 
TDD stands for Test Driven Development. Test Driven Development is a software development process where test cases are written first taking into consideration the requirements in a traditional project or the user stories in a scrum or agile project. Once the tests are created, minimal code to make the tests pass is created. As and when new tests are created, the code is updated to make the new tests pass and at the same time ensuring that the existing tests pass as well.
 
TDD (We will refer to this acronym for Test Driven Development going forward) was developed or rediscovered by Kent Beck in 2003 to facilitate simple designs. TDD is related to test first programming concepts of Extreme Programming.

 
1.1.1 Steps involved in a TDD
 
The steps mentioned below should be followed in a typical Test Driven Development approach.
  
Write the This activity can be done by the tester or developer where a test is created from the user story, requirement or use case. This is contrasted to the traditional approach of writing unit tests after the code is written. TDD enables the developer to focus on the requirements (We will refer to user stories, traditional requirements or use cases as requirements going forward) before getting started with the code. This differentiated TDD from a traditional development approach.
 
Run the test to check that it Prepare the development system such that bare minimum code is there to make your application run like creating the main method or a screen with the required stubs for the database or web service for example. Since writing the test was the very first activity done, it should definitely fail since we don't have any code in place to support the test. If the test fails, then we are sure that the test has been written correctly.
 
Write the development Now it's time to make our test pass by writing only the required code to make the test pass. It is strongly recommended not to write more code in this step. Writing more code results in what is called Gold Plating where you are just giving additional features that are not required at the present moment.
 
Check to see that the test Run our first test again and this time it should pass. This helps to ensure that all the correct development code is in place and we can move on to the next test.
 
Refactor the In the iterative TDD process, we need to make sure that we have not introduced any duplication, all the design principles are met and the methods are where they are supposed to be, that is, logically grouped together in a class.
 
Repeat with new Next we write new tests for new requirements and repeat steps 1-5 to ensure that the correct code is written and only the required code is written. TDD will help you build a near defect free application using the minimum amount of code. There are many tools in the market for TDD one of them being JUnit. Since this book is focussed on BDD, we won’t go into details about testing with JUnit.

 
1.2 What is BDD?
 
BDD is an extension of TDD that makes use of a simple, Domain Specific Language The DSL is in plain English and convert natural language statements into executable tests. The DSL that we are going to study in this book is known by the name Gherkin. The term Gherkin however is specific to Cucumber, JBehave, Behave and Behat software tools.
 
BDD focuses on:
  
Where to start
 
What to test and what to exclude
 
How much to test
 
What to name the tests
 
Understanding why a test fails
 
Let's get our hands dirty with the first DSL in Gherkin.
  
Cash withdrawal from ATM
 
Successful cash withdrawal
 
Given the account balance is $100
 
And the card is valid
 
And the ATM contains sufficient money
 
When the account holder requests $20
 
Then the cashslot should dispense $20
 
And the account balance should be $80
 
And the card should be returned
  
These very simple English statements can be split into three distinct sections.
  
Context: This defines the starting state
 
 
Figure 1.1: Example of Given keyword
 
Event: This defines the user's action or actions
 
 
Figure 1.2: Example of When keyword
 
Outcomes: This defines the expected results
 
 
Figure 1.3: Example of ‘Then’ and ‘And’ keywords
  
The words highlighted in Bold like ‘’‘’’’“Given”, “When”, “Then” and ‘’“And‘’ are known as Cucumber
 
Let’s have a look at each of these keywords
  
The purpose of Given is to put the system in a known state before the user starts interacting with the system.
 
The purpose of When steps is to describe the key action the user performs.
 
The purpose of Then steps is to observe outcomes. The observations should be related in some way to the business value in your feature description. The observations should also be on some kind of output – that is values that come out of the system.
 
Used to connect multiple Given, When and Then steps.
 
The above Domain Specific Language has the Feature and Scenario steps also. We will cover each of these steps in detail when we start designing the Page Object Model Framework. We are now ready to get introduced to Cucumber.

 
1.3 What is Cucumber?
 
Cucumber is a tool based on the BDD Framework. Cucumber makes use of Gherkin keywords. Gherkin is a DSL which is used in Cucumber to create test cases. Rather than building linear pieces of code, it is best to understand Cucumber by building a framework of some sort. The framework that can be used for Cucumber is Page Object which is based on the Page Object Design Pattern. We will understand the Page Object Pattern throughout this book, but let’s understand how Cucumber is structured and once we understand that, we will go deeper into understanding how Cucumber fits into the Page Object Model Framework. To get a feel of Cucumber, you may visit www.cucumber.io which gives much detail about Cucumber.

 
1.3.1 Structure of Cucumber
 
Cucumber comprises three components viz. Runner class, Feature Files and Step Definition classes. Ideally in a scenario where you have no framework, these are all the components you need to execute Cucumber feature file scenarios. Generally, projects are implemented using Frameworks and in the case of Page Object Model Framework, apart from the three mandatory components mentioned above, we have another set called Page Object These are Java classes with each page in the Application Under Test corresponding to one Page object class. Thus there is one to one correspondence between Page Objects and Pages in the AUT. When we start designing page objects, we will see how to utilize the concept of inheritance to keep code clean and to avoid code duplication. A very important principle exists known as Don’t Repeat Yourself which we will see next. Generally, the default language for the Test Runner class is JUNIT but in this book we will see how to use TestNG for driving the framework. Just because we will use TestNG, we will also make use of TestNG xml to drive the framework. For creating Test Suites in Cucumber, we will make use of something called Using Tags proves to be extremely helpful while working with test suites.

 
1.4 Understanding the DRY principle
 
‘DRY’ simply means Don’t Repeat Yourself. What this means is that we write the methods pertaining to web elements on a web page in one class. These methods can pertain to clicking a button or entering values in a test box. To be precise, that one class will have as many methods as there are web elements.
 
So rather
 
We would write something like the code line shown below in the class which corresponds to the webpage. Suppose we are dealing with the login page and there is a button with id as ‘Login’
 
WebElement btnLogin = driver.findElement(By.id(’Login’));
clickLogin(btnLogin);
 
This is always better than doing something like this everywhere in your tests where the Login page is involved.
 
Driver.findElement(By.id(’Login’)).click();
 
The hard coded value can be replaced by dynamic or static locators which we will see when we look at Page Objects.

 
1.5 Components of Cucumber Framework
 
As every other framework, Cucumber also has well defined components. Cucumber has three main components which are Runner class, Feature Files and Step Definition files. Apart from these basic components, we will be using Maven and Jenkins. We will learn about Maven and Jenkins in subsequent chapters but now we mainly focus on the three main components which are Runner class, Feature Files, and Step Definition files.

 
1.5.1 Runner class
 
This is the class that triggers the framework. The components of the class are given as follows:
  
This is used on top of the Runner class and helps in specifying where our Feature files, Step Definition files, plugins for report generation like Pretty (for HTML reports), JSON or Rerun.
 
TestNGCucumberRunner We create a reference to this class called TestNGCucumberRunner inside the TestRunner class. We create a new instance of TesrNGCucumberRunner passing the parameter as inside a method annotated with Similar to we will have a teardown method with @AfterClass annotation where we will invoke the finish() method on the TesrNGCucumberRunner instance.
 
Methods with @Test We can also have test methods that can optionally take data from a data provider. Assigning of groups can also be done for the test methods.
 
DataProvider DataProvider methods with the @DataProvider annotation can be designed which can pull data from the data tables present in the feature files.

 
1.5.2 Feature Files
 
Feature files are our test cases in simple words. These test cases can be designed by anyone in the team and are in simple English language. The extension of Feature files is The language used in the feature file is called Gherkin which is English like and contains keywords like ‘GIVEN’,’WHEN’, ‘THEN’, ‘OR’, ‘BUT’, and so on. We have already seen the structure of feature files earlier in this chapter. Chapter 2, Understanding Feature Files is dedicated to Feature files.

 
1.5.3 Step Definition Files
 
These are files that get generated for us with dummy methods when we run the feature file by right clicking on the feature file in Eclipse and clicking As Cucumber The dummy step definition methods look like this:
 
@Given(“^User is on the home page$”)
Public void user_is_on_the_home_page() throws Throwable {
Throw new PendingException();
}
 
The user has to add code at the place where it says new The name of the method is immaterial. The methods will be executed based on the match of the regular expression with that of the feature file. So in this case, there should be a Gherkin keyword ‘GIVEN’ in the feature file followed by is on the home Chapter 3, Step Definitions is dedicated to Step Definition files.
 
Apart from these three components, there might be Java classes that act as page objects. There has to be one java class for each screen or page.

CHAPTER 2
 
Understanding Feature Files
 
We will begin by understanding the components of the Cucumber framework in this chapter with the first component which is feature files. Feature files are mostly written in plain English but can be written in other supported languages. They specify a business requirement, for example, logging into a web application and verifying whether the title is correct. This business requirement is specified as a sequence of steps which instruct the system of what action has to be taken in order to fulfil the business requirement.
 
We will thoroughly understand the different components of a feature file. We will start from a basic feature with one scenario and later build multiple scenarios with different steps using Gherkin keywords like Given, When, Then, And, But, and so on. The reader will understand how easy it is to learn Cucumber feature files and can start developing complex feature files.
 
This chapter will predominantly focus on:
  
Feature files
 
Creating feature files
 
Plug-in for Feature files
 
Introducing feature, Scenario, and Scenario outline
 
Understanding the different keywords
 
Reusing the same step with different arguments
 
Using complex data types
 
Understanding DocStrings
 
Background step
 
Feature file in a different language
 
Designing complex feature files
 
Introducing Tags

 
Objectives
 
After reading this chapter, the reader will be able to:
  
Create complex feature files.
 
Understand the concepts of Scenario and Scenario outline.
 
Learn how to pass arguments in steps.
 
Understand the usage of complex data types.
 
Grasp the concepts of feature files using examples

 
2.1 What are feature files?
 
Feature files are files that have tests written in a descriptive language like English. It is the entry point for the Cucumber framework. Of course, to execute our tests from Jenkins, we will put a testNG.xml and a Runner class with cucumber tags. This will form a layer over the feature file.
 
The following is a sample feature file to log in to the freecrm website:
 
Feature: To test login functionality to www.freecrm.com
Scenario: To test a successful login
Given User navigates to the login page
When User enters “admin” as username
And User enters “admin” as password
And User clicks the Login button
Then User should be shown User Name on top left corner
 
A feature file contains certain in-built keywords like ‘Feature’, ‘Scenario’, ‘Given’, ‘When’, ‘And’, ‘But’, ‘Then’, and so on. These are keywords defined in a language known as Gherkin. Gherkin has more keywords apart from the ones shown here, but we will go with the ones mentioned here and understand what each keyword does.

2.2 Introducing feature, scenario, and scenario outline
 
A feature file consists of the following keywords: Feature and Scenario or Scenario outline. Let’s understand each keyword in detail.

 
2.2.1 Feature
 
In Cucumber, feature files specify business needs or requirements. The title of the feature file immediately follows the feature keyword and is on the same line. Three (optional) text lines may follow the line having the feature keyword and specify the intent of the feature file. Feature files contain Scenario or Scenario Outline.

 
2.2.2 Scenario
 
Scenarios are similar to test cases in manual testing. They start with the Scenario keyword in a new line (other than the one in which the feature intent is present). The Scenario Title follows the Scenario keyword and is on the same line as that of the keyword. The Intent of the Scenario is specified by three (optional) lines following the line in which the Scenario keyword is present.
 
A Scenario consists of steps which make use of keywords like and so on.
 
An example of a Scenario is shown as follows:
 
To test the login functionality to www.freecrm.com
 
To test a successful login:
 
Given User navigates to the login page
 
When User enters as username
 
And User enters as password
 
And User clicks the Login button
 
Then User should be shown User Name on top left corner
 
Let’s explore Scenario Outline next.

 
2.2.3 Scenario Outline
 
Scenario Outline is used to execute the same scenario multiple times with different sets of values. Consider the following two scenarios:
 
To test login functionality to www.freecrm.com
 
To test a successful login
 
Given User navigates to the login page
 
When User enters as username
 
And User enters as password
 
And User clicks the Login button
 
Then User should be shown User Name on top left corner
 
To test a successful login
 
Given User navigates to the login page
 
When User enters as username
 
And User enters as password
 
And User clicks the Login button
 
Then User should be shown User Name on top left corner
 
Notice that the second scenario is a redundant one. To eliminate this redundancy, we make use of Scenario Outline shown as follows. We will have 2 iterations for this feature. One for and the other for
 
To test login functionality to www.freecrm.com
 
Scenario To test a successful login
 
Given User navigates to the login page
 
When User enters as username
 
And User enters as password
 
And User clicks the Login button
 
Then User should be shown User Name on top left corner
 
 
      | userName                    | password               |
      | admin                           | admin                     |
      | superuser                     | superuser              |
 
We now move on to understand what each keyword (GIVEN, WHEN, THEN, and so on) mean.

 
2.3 Understanding the different keywords
 
In this section, we will understand the meaning of the different keywords used in a Scenario.
 
This keyword establishes the initial state of the Application under Test so that the subsequent steps will perform operations on the AUT. An example of the Given keyword is given as follows:
 
Given User navigates to the login page
 
This keyword describes the user action. An example of the When keyword is given as follows:
 
When User enters “” as username
 
This keyword describes the expected result. An example of the Then keyword is given as follows:
 
Then User should be shown User Name on top left corner
 
This keyword is used for statements that add to the previous Step/Steps and represent positive statements.
 
And User enters “superuser” as password
 
This keyword is used for statements that add to the previous Step/Steps and represent negative statements.
 
But I should not see "Admin" as the role

 
2.4 Reusing the same step with different arguments
 
Suppose we have two scenarios where we need to check different sets of data shown as follows:
 
To test a successful login
 
Given User navigates to the login page
 
When User enters as username
 
And User enters as password
 
And User clicks the Login button
 
Then User should be shown User Name on top left corner
 
To test a successful login
 
Given User navigates to the login page
 
When User enters as username
 
And User enters as password
 
And User clicks the Login button
 
Then User should be shown User Name on top left corner
 
When these scenarios are executed, the flow of control passes into a Step Definition file where we will see a method similar to the one as follows:
 
@When("^User enters \"(.*?)\" as username$")
public void User_enters_as_username(String userName) {
//print the value of data passed from Feature file
System.out.println(userName);
}
 
Output:
 
admin
superuser
 
The \"(.*?)\" in the preceding code is known as a Regular Let’s understand each part of this regular expression.
  
‘*’ represents zero or more occurrences of the preceding element.
 
‘?’ represents zero or one occurrences of the preceding element.
 
‘.’ represents a single character except the NewLine character.
 
We will understand new regular expressions as and when we encounter them.

 
2.5 Using complex data types
 
In this section, we will use a table with a step shown as follows. The ‘Then’ step runs three times with different usernames.
 
To test a successful login
 
Given User navigates to the login page
 
Then Verify that following users are able to Login
 
| userName    | password  |
| KamleshP    | xyz       |
| RamK        | abc       |
| MikeP       | mkpe      |
 
The corresponding step definition contains the following method. Here, we make use of the DataTable to pull the step table data into a List of String:
 
@Then("^Verify that following users are able to Login$")
public void verify_that_following_users_are_able_to_Login(DataTable loginDetails){
//Write the code to handle Data Table
List> loginData = loginDetails.raw();
System.out.println(loginData.get(1).get(0));
}
 
Output:
 
KamleshP

 
2.6 Understanding DocStrings
 
Doc Strings are large text paragraphs in the feature file which are enclosed within """ (Three quotes). For example, consider the feature file shown below. Please note that this is just an example. The actual www.freecrm.com does not contain this text.
 
To test login functionality to www.freecrm.com
 
Scenario Outline: To test a successful login
 
Given User navigates to the login page
 
When User enters as username
 
And User enters as password
 
And User clicks the Login button
 
Then User should be shown this paragraph
 
"""
 
Welcome to freecrm, your one stop solution for all your HR needs
 
"""
 
We will see how to incorporate the doc strings functionality in Java code when we study about step definition files in the next chapter.

 
2.7 Background Script
 
A Background script runs before each scenario and looks as follows:
 
 
Given User navigates to the login page
 
When User enters as username
 
And User enters as password
 
And User clicks the Login button
 
Here, the background step executes before each scenario in a feature file. Let’s take the case where the Contact and Deal scenario are in the same feature file.
 
To test Contact and Deal creation functionality
 
To test a successful contact creation
 
Given User navigates to the login page
 
When User enters as username
 
And User enters as password
 
And User clicks the Login button
 
And User creates a new Contact
 
Then User should be shown Contact Confirmation page
 
To test a successful Deal creation
 
Given User navigates to the login page
 
When User enters as username
 
And User enters as password
 
And User clicks the Login button
 
And User creates a new Deal
 
Then User should be shown Deal Confirmation page
 
Once we add the background step, the feature file would look like the one shown as follows:
 
To test Contact and Deal creation functionality
 
 
Given User navigates to the login page
 
When User enters as username
 
And User enters as password
 
And User clicks the Login button
 
To test a successful contact creation
 
Given User creates a new Contact
 
Then User should be shown Contact Confirmation page
 
To test a successful Deal creation
 
Given User creates a new Deal
 
Then User should be shown Deal Confirmation page
 
When the feature file shown above is executed, the background script runs before each scenario executes and acts as a prerequisite for each scenario in the feature file. We will see this in action when we learn about Step Definition files.

 
2.8 Feature files in a different language
 
We work in different Geographies in outsourced projects and not everyone understands feature files written in English. Cucumber supports 40 different languages for its feature file. If we need to create the feature file in a language other than English, we have to do two things
  
Include the header # language: xyz as the first line of the feature file
 
Save the file with UTF-8 encoding.
 
The following code is a feature file in Norwegian:
 
# language: no
Funksjonalitet: Gjett et ord
 
Eksempel: Ordmaker starter et spill
Når Ordmaker starter et spill
Så må Ordmaker vente på at Gjetter blir med
 
Eksempel: Gjetter blir med
Gitt at Ordmaker har startet et spill med ordet "bløtt"
Når Gjetter blir med på Ordmakers spill
Så må Gjetter gjette et ord på 5 bokstaver

We will take a look at how to work with basic and complex feature files using the Step Definition files in the next chapter, although a small excerpt of a Step Definition file was covered in this chapter.
 
We now move to the final topic of this chapter which is Tags.

 
2.10 Understanding Cucumber tags
 
We can create test suites in Cucumber using what are called Tags are written starting with ‘@’ followed by the tag name shown as follows. If you notice, the @Regression tag applies to the entire feature and @Sanity and @Negative apply to individual Scenarios. For now, just remember this syntax. We will look at executing these when we look at the TestRunner class. Moreover, we will also see inheritance in feature files.
@Regression
 
To test login functionality to www.freecrm.com
 
@Smoke
 
To test a successful login
 
Given User navigates to the login page
 
When User enters as username

To test a unsuccessful login with incorrect username
 
Given User navigates to the login page

To test a unsuccessful login with incorrect password
 
Given User navigates to the login page

And User enters as password

Then User should be shown the login page

CHAPTER 3
 
Step Definitions
 
We will learn about the second component of Cucumber which is Step Definitions. Step Definition files are the glue code between feature files and Page Object classes. Creating Step Definition files is not an overhead because Cucumber auto generates these files for us. We will use the Step Definition files to pass the control flow from feature files to Page Object classes.
 
We will understand different components of a Step Definition like and and learn how to implement DocStrings. We will start from Step Definition for a basic feature with one scenario and later build Step Definitions for multiple scenarios with different steps. The reader will be able to speed up with building Step Definitions for a given feature file after reading this chapter.
 
This chapter will predominantly focus on:
  
Step Definitions
 
Auto-generate Step Definitions
 
Understanding optional Capture/Non-Capture groups
 
Handling string and integer arguments
 
Implementing DataTables
 
Handling DocStrings
 
Handling Scenario Outline Data Tables
 
Duplicate Step Definitions
 
Cucumber Hooks

 
Objectives
 
After reading this chapter, the reader will be able to create Step Definitions which connect to the feature files via regular expressions. He will understand the concepts of designing Step Definitions for Scenario and Scenario outline which consist of a table attached to a step and a Scenario outline table with the keyword. He will learn how to handle arguments that are passed in steps of a feature file. By grasping the creation of effective Step Definitions, the reader will be able to quickly build automated test cases using just feature files and Step Definitions.

 
3.1 What are Step Definitions?
 
Step Definition is also called Glue code since it forms the glue between the feature files and JavaPage Object classes. These step definitions are a combination of Java code along with regular expressions.
 
Here is a sample feature file to log in to the freecrm website. Create a new feature file BPB_1.feature in the featurefiles folder in
 
To test login functionality to www.freecrm.com
 
To test a successful login
 
Given User navigates to the login page
 
When User enters as username
 
And User enters as password
 
And User clicks the Login button
 
Then User should be shown User Name on top left corner
 
In order for this feature to work, the corresponding glue code should be created. The next section explains how to auto-generate this code in an IDE.

 
3.1.1 Auto generating the Step Definition code in an IDE
 
Open Eclipse IDE and go to package called In this package, create a file called feature1.feature and enter the steps shown in section In the Project explorer window of Eclipse, right click on the Feature file and select Run As | Cucumber In the console window in Eclipse, the following code gets auto-generated. Note that this is just a template code that is provided by the IDE and each of the methods throws a Pending Exception:
 
@Given("^User navigates to the login page$")
public void user_navigates_to_the_login_page() throws Throwable {
// Write code here that turns the phrase above into concrete actions
throw new PendingException();
}
 
@When("^User enters \"([^\"]*)\" as username$")
public void user_enters_as_username(String arg1) throws Throwable {
// Write code here that turns the phrase above into concrete actions
throw new PendingException();
}
 
@When("^User enters \"([^\"]*)\" as password$")
public void user_enters_as_password(String arg1) throws Throwable {
// Write code here that turns the phrase above into concrete actions
throw new PendingException();
}
 
@When("^User clicks the Login button$")
public void user_clicks_the_Login_button() throws Throwable {
// Write code here that turns the phrase above into concrete actions
throw new PendingException();
}
 
@Then("^User should be shown User Name on top left corner$")
public void user_should_be_shown_User_Name_on_top_left_corner() throws Throwable {
// Write code here that turns the phrase above into concrete actions
throw new PendingException();
}
 
In the stepdefinitions folder, create a Java class called and add the preceding code with modifications shown as follows:
 
public class BPB_1 {
 
@Given("^User navigates to the login page$")
public void user_navigates_to_the_login_page() throws Throwable {
System.out.println("Navigated to Login Page");
}
 
@When("^User enters \"(.*?)\" as username$")
public void user_enters_admin_as_username(String userName) throws Throwable {
System.out.println("UserName is: "+userName);
}
 
@And("^User enters \"(.*?)\" as password$")
public void user_enters_admin_as_password(String password) throws Throwable {
System.out.println("Password is: "+password);
}
 
@And("^User clicks the Login button$")
public void user_clicks_the_Login_button() throws Throwable {
System.out.println("Login button clicked");
}
 
@Then("^User should be shown User Name on top left corner$")
public void user_should_be_shown_User_Name_on_top_left_corner() throws Throwable {
System.out.println("UserName verified");
}
}
 
The output is displayed in the following screenshot:
 
 
Figure 3.1: Output from the Step definition
 
Note that the username and password get substituted as and the step definition takes this value from the feature file. This value is accepted by a regular expression of the form:
 
@When("^User enters \"(.*?)\" as username$")
 
Here \"(.*?)\" is known as a regular expression which is used to pass in arguments from the feature file. Let’s understand Capture Groups next.

 
3.2 Understanding optional Capture/Non-Capture groups
 
Think about a situation where we have multiple business analysts creating feature files. We will understand and groups with an example.

 
3.2.1 Capture groups
 
Let’s take an example of a step written in two different ways:
  
Given User navigates to the login page.
   
Given User goes to the login page.
  
Here, only one word differs in the step which is and Apart from that, the step is the same. An efficient step definition shown below takes the action written in the feature file and prints it out. Alter BPB_1.java for the code snippet shown as follows:
 
@Given("^User (navigates|goes) to the login page$")
public void user_navigates_to_the_login_page(String entry) throws Throwable {
System.out.println("Navigated to Login Page with verb "+entry);
}
 
The output will look as follows:
 
With the first step, we get the output shown as follows:
 
Navigated to Login Page with verb navigates
 
With the second Given step, we get the output shown as follows:
 
Navigated to Login Page with verb goes
 
In the preceding Step Definition, we had to mention an argument for the method. It is not likely that this verb (navigates or goes) will be used anywhere else in the business logic. Here, the verb (navigates or goes) forms a capture group as shown in the regular expression as follows:
 
@Given("^User (navigates|goes) to the login page$")
 
What if we do not want to pass the verb as an argument but still wish to keep the feature files untouched. We need a Non-Capture group in that case.

 
3.2.2 Non-Capture groups
 
Consider the same Given step of section Non-Capture groups provide the ability to specify different verbs. For example, (navigates|goes) in the feature file without having to pass it as an argument in the Step Definition. The change that needs to be done in BPB_1.java in the regular expression of the method in the Step Definition is shown as follows:
 
@Given("^User to the login page$")
public void user_navigates_to_the_login_page() throws Throwable {
System.out.println("Navigated to Login Page");
}
 
Output: Navigated to Login Page is printed to the console.
 
The Non-Capture group is mentioned in the regular expression attached to the method with a preceding ‘?:’. Anything that follows this symbol is considered as a non-capture group, and hence, it need not be passed as an argument to the method as shown above.

 
3.3 Handling string and integer arguments
 
We have already seen how to handle String arguments in the few examples given above. Let’s take an example of a feature file that contains both String and Integer arguments passed in it. Alter BPB_1.java with the contents as follows:
 
Feature: To test login functionality to www.freecrm.com
 
Scenario: To test a successful login
 
Given User navigates to the login page
 
When User enters "admin" as username
 
And User enters "admin" as password
 
And User enters 12345 as pin
 
And User clicks the Login button
 
Then User should be shown User Name on top left corner
 
Consider the highlighted steps in bold. The corresponding step definition methods from BPB_1.java for those are given as follows:
 
@And("^User enters \"(.*?)\" as password$")
public void user_enters_admin_as_password(String password) throws Throwable {
System.out.println("Password is: "+password);
}
 
@And("^User enters (\\d+) as pin$")
public void user_enters_as_password(int pin) throws Throwable {
// Write code here that turns the phrase above into concrete actions
System.out.println("Pin is: "+pin);
}
 
The output is as follows:
 
Password is: admin
Pin is: 12345
 
Note that the regular expression for an integer argument is specified as (\\d+). The ‘+’ stands for one or more occurrences.

 
3.4 Implementing Data Tables
 
In this section, we will see how to implement Scenario DataTables. The following feature file has a Scenario DataTable:
 
Feature: Test for a DataTable
 
Scenario: To test a successful login
Given User navigates to the login page
Then Verify that following users are able to Login
| userName | password |
| KamleshP | xyz      |
| RamK     | abc      |
| MikeP    | mkpe     |
 
Create a class BPB_2.java and add the code shown as follows:
 
@Then("^Verify that following users are able to Login$")
public void verify_that_following_users_are_able_to_Login(DataTable
loginDetails) throws Throwable {
List> loginData = loginDetails.raw();
for (int i=1;i{
System.out.println("The usernames in the data table are "+loginData.get(i).get(0));
}
}
 
Output:
 
The usernames in the data table are KamleshP
The usernames in the data table are RamK
The usernames in the data table are MikeP
 
DataTables are passed to the Step Definition as the last argument. It is required to import the following in order to make this code to execute:
 
import cucumber.api.DataTable;
import cucumber.api.java.en.And;
import cucumber.api.java.en.Given;
import cucumber.api.java.en.Then;
import cucumber.api.java.en.When;
 
The raw() method of the DataTable API is used to convert the DataTable into a list of String.

3.8 Cucumber Hooks
 
Sometimes, we may need to execute actions before and after all the steps of the feature file. This can be implemented using Hooks in Cucumber. Unlike TestNG, Cucumber only supports two hooks which are @Before and The method annotated by @Before gets executed before any step of the feature file is executed and @After gets executed after all steps of the feature file are executed. Add the following methods to
 
@Before
public void setUp() {
System.out.println("Before any of the methods");
}
 
@After
public void tearDown() {
System.out.println("After all methods");
}
 
Now, try executing BPB_1.feature and we get the output as follows:

Navigated to Login Page
UserName is: admin
Password is: admin
Pin is: 12345
Login button clicked
UserName verified
After all methods

4.1 What is the Singleton Pattern?
 
The single design pattern is one of the creational design patterns in Java. It is used to create an object in Java. Only one instance exists at a given time when the Singleton Pattern is used. Other classes that utilize this class have access to only one instance of this class. The Singleton pattern saves memory since the same instance is utilized time and again.
 
This pattern is implemented with the use of the components shown as follows:
  
Static member This holds the instance of the Singleton class. It saves memory as it is static.
 
Private This prevents instantiation of the class from outside using the new keyword.
 
Static Factory This can be accessed using This method returns the instance of the Singleton class to the caller.
 
The Singleton pattern is used in test automation for the WebDriver instance creation. Apart from this in development, it is used in Database and Multi-Threaded applications. It is also used in thread pools, caching, logging, and so on.
 
We will take a look at how we can make our code thread-safe in the next section.

 
4.2 Introduction to the ThreadLocal class in Java
 
We will now take a look at how we can achieve parallel execution in Selenium. We will make use of parallel execution features of TestNG which requires the creation of a separate thread for each driver instance. The ThreadLocal class of Java will be utilized for this purpose. By declaring variables as shown in the following code, we make sure that each thread has its own copy of the WebDriver instance:
 
ThreadLocal driver = new ThreadLocal();
 
Apart from the Driver instance, we will have the variables which hold the session ID, Browser name, the platform (Windows or Linux), and the Version:
 
private ThreadLocal sessId = new ThreadLocal();
private ThreadLocal sBrwsr = new ThreadLocal();
private ThreadLocal sPltfrm = new ThreadLocal();
private ThreadLocal sVrsn = new ThreadLocal();
 
Each of these variables is thread-safe. Note that in section 4.1, when were introduced to the Singleton pattern which can be used to initiate a single browser session throughout. Here, we make the driver instance thread safe, thus giving an opportunity to launch multiple driver instances. Next, we will take a look at the WebDriverManager library which helps us in automating the driver binary management.

 
4.3 Introducing the WebDriverManager library
 
Enter the code shown as follows in the Main method:
 
System. setProperty("webdriver.chrome.driver", "path of the exe file\\chromedriver.exe");
WebDriver driver=new ChromeDriver();
 
This will open a Chrome browser session. The driver executable has to be downloaded manually. This works fine but the problem with this is that every time the Chrome browser gets an update, the version of the driver executable has to be changed. Suppose testing has to be done on a specific version of a browser. This is not possible when we have to download the driver executable manually.
 
The WebDriverManager library helps us in this by automatic management of the driver executable. WebDriverManager comes as a Maven dependency shown as follows:
 
io.github.bonigarcia
webdrivermanager
3.6.2
 
Right click on the project and select Maven | Update Project.
 
The following lines
 
System. setProperty("webdriver.chrome.driver", "path of the exe file\\chromedriver.exe");
WebDriver driver=new ChromeDriver();
 
Will be replaced with the following:
 
WebDriverManager.chromedriver().setup();
WebDriver chromeDriver = new ChromeDriver();
 
Execute this code and you will see a Chrome browser opening with the console output shown as follows:
 
 
Figure 4.1: WebDriverManager output for Chrome browser

4.4 Design a Singleton WebDriver using the WebDriverManager library
 
Since we have seen concepts such as Singleton pattern, the ThreadLocal class, and the WebDriverManager library, we can now design the Singleton WebDriver class. Instead of looking at the full code, we will look at the individual methods for ease of understanding. We have already seen the ThreadLocal variables that will be used in this class in section

 
4.4.1 Private Constructor
 
The Singleton WebDriver class will have a private constructor so that this class cannot be instantiated from outside using the new() keyword. The constructor is shown as follows:
 
// Private constructor in order to block instantiation of this class from outside
private SingletonDriver() {
}
 
We now look at how to fetch the Single instance of the SingletonDriver class.

 
4.4.2 Fetching the Singleton class instance
 
The next component of the SingletonDriver class is the method to fetch the Singleton instance of the driver class so that it can be accessed from outside.
 
/**
* getInstance method will fetch the active driver instance
*
* @return SingletoDriver
*/
public static SingletonDriver getInstance() {
if (instance == null) {
instance = new SingletonDriver();
}
return instance;
}
 
We will next look at setting the Driver and its preferences with the setDrvr method.

 
4.4.3 Setting the Driver and its preferences
 
The next component of the SingletonDriver class is the method to set the Singleton instance of the driver class to Chrome, Firefox, or Internet Explorer based on the arguments passed to the setDrvr method. We will use WebDriverManager to instantiate the drivers. Here, we will also set the browser, platform, and environment to the respective ThreadLocal variables. The code is as follows:
 
/**
* setDrvr method to create driver instance
* Parameters are mentioned below
* browser
* environment
* platform
* optPreferences
* also throws Exception
*/
@SafeVarargs
public final void setDrvr(String brwsr, String pltfrm, String envrnmnt, MapObject>... optPrefs) throws Exception {
DesiredCapabilities caps = null;
String getPltfrm = null;
props.load(new FileInputStream(GLOBAL_DATA.SE_PROPRTS));
switch (brwsr) {
case "firefox":
caps = DesiredCapabilities.firefox();
FirefoxOptions ffOpts = new FirefoxOptions();
FirefoxProfile ffProfile = new FirefoxProfile();
ffProfile.setPreference("browser.autofocus", true);
ffProfile.setPreference("browser.tabs.remote.autostart.2", false);
caps.setCapability(FirefoxDriver.PROFILE, ffProfile);
caps.setCapability("marionette", true);
// then pass them to the local WebDriver
if (envrnmnt.equalsIgnoreCase("local")) {
WebDriverManager.firefoxdriver().setup();
webDriver.set(new
FirefoxDriver(ffOpts.merge(caps)));
}
break;
case "chrome":
caps = DesiredCapabilities.chrome();
ChromeOptions chOptions = new ChromeOptions();
MapObject> chromePrefs =
new HashMapObject>();
chromePrefs.put("credentials_enable_service", false);
chOptions.setExperimentalOption("prefs", chromePrefs);
chOptions.addArguments("--disable-plugins", "--disable-extensions", "--disable-popup-blocking");
caps.setCapability(ChromeOptions.CAPABILITY, chOptions);
caps.setCapability("applicationCacheEnabled", false);
if (envrnmnt.equalsIgnoreCase("local")) {
WebDriverManager.chromedriver().setup();
webDriver.set(new
ChromeDriver(chOptions.merge(caps)));
}
break;
case "internet explorer":
caps = DesiredCapabilities.internetExplorer();
InternetExplorerOptions ieOpts =
new InternetExplorerOptions();
ieOpts.requireWindowFocus();
ieOpts.merge(caps);
caps.setCapability("requireWindowFocus", true);
if (envrnmnt.equalsIgnoreCase("local")) {
WebDriverManager.iedriver().setup();
webDriver.set(new InternetExplorerDriver(
ieOpts.merge(caps)));
}
break;
}
getEnv = envrnmnt;
getPltfrm = pltfrm;
 
sessId.set(((RemoteWebDriver) webDriver.get())
.getSessionId().toString());
 
sBrwsr.set(caps.getBrowserName());
sVrsn.set(caps.getVersion());
sPltfrm.set(getPltfrm);
System.out.println("\n*** THE TEST ENVIRONMENT DETAILS ARE "
+ getSessBrwsr().toUpperCase()
+ "||" + getSessPltfrm().toUpperCase()
+ "||" + getEnv.toUpperCase()
+ "||Selenium Version is"
+ props.getProperty("selenium.revision")
+ "||Session ID="
+ getSessId()
+ "\n");
getDrvr().manage().timeouts().implicitlyWait(
IMPLCT_TIMEOUT, TimeUnit.SECONDS);
getDrvr().manage().window().maximize();
}
 
Next, we have a look at fetching the WebDriver instance.

 
4.4.4 Fetching the WebDriver instance
 
The following method is used to fetch the active WebDriver instance. The method used to fetch the instance is get() which is invoked on the WebDriver instance. The code is as follows:

* getDriver method to fetch active driver

return webDriver.get();

The other preferences can be fetched in a similar fashion. Finally, we have the code to close the browser.

4.6 Introduction to the Test Runner class
 
The Test Runner is the point in our framework where we have details like the location of the Feature files, Step Definitions, Reporting configurations, and tags. Apart from this, the Test Runner class will extend a class called We have a test method for executing the steps in the feature file. In case there is a data table that provides data to the feature, we have a data provider method. We also have a private variable of type private TestNGCucumberRunner which is declared as follows:
 
private TestNGCucumberRunner;
 
The steps from the feature file are read by the Data Provider and read by the CucumberFeatureWrapper parameter. The runCucumber method of the TestNGCucumberRunner takes in one argument which has the Feature file data that can be pulled using the getCucumberFeature() method.
 
@Test(dataProvider="features")
public void feature(CucumberFeatureWrapper cucumberFeature) {
testNGCucumberRunner.runCucumber(cucumberFeature.getCucumberFeature());
}
 
The following code is our DataProvider which returns a two-dimensional Object Array of the data of the Feature file, including the DataTable data. We will first instantiate an object of TestNGCucumberRunner if it is null and return the Feature file data using the provideFeatures() method:
 
@DataProvider
public Object[][] features() {
if(testNGCucumberRunner == null){
testNGCucumberRunner = new TestNGCucumberRunner(this.getClass());
}
return testNGCucumberRunner.provideFeatures();
}
 
The preceding feature() method is executed for all steps and iterations of every feature. The output is shown in the following screenshot:
 
 
Figure 4.2: Output of the Test Runner
 
Apart from the output shown here, browser sessions of Chrome are opened and closed twice since we have two executions for 2 scenarios.
 
Please Note: To execute this TestRunner class, we will make use of the TestNG xml shown in the following code. We will explore this xml when we learn about TestNG in the upcoming chapters.
 
version="1.0" encoding="UTF-8"?>
suite SYSTEM "http://testng.org/testng-1.0.dtd">
name="Suite">
thread-count="5" name="Test">
name="testrunner.BPBTR_1"/>

4.8 Opening the browser of your choice
 
Let’s create a feature file with just one step for opening the browser of our choice. We have explicitly mentioned in the Given step which browser to open, on which platform, and whether it will be used with Selenium Grid:
 
@Single
Feature: Open browser of choice
I want to open browser of my choice
Scenario: Open browser of choice
Given I open the "chrome" browser on "windows" and "local"
 
The corresponding Step Definition which invokes the setDrvr() method of the SingletonDriver class is shown as follows:
 
public class BPBSD_00 {
@Given("^I open the \"([^\"]*)\" browser on \"([^\"]*)\" and \"([^\"]*)\"$")
public void i_open_the_browser(String browserName, String platform, String gridSetting) throws Throwable {
// Write code here that turns the phrase above into concrete actions
try {
SingletonDriver.getInstance().setDrvr(browserName, platform, gridSetting, null);
} catch (Exception e) {
// TODO Auto-generated catch block
e.printStackTrace();
}
}
}
 
Please note that the @Before annotation from section 4.6 should be removed prior to running this code otherwise two Chrome browser sessions will be opened.

 
4.9 Quitting the driver instance
 
In order to quit the browser after a Feature file execution, create a Step Definition file BPBSD_99 and write the code as follows:
 
public class BPBSD_99 {
@After
public void tearDown() {
System.out.println("After all methods");
SingletonDriver.getInstance().closeDriver();
}
}
 
Here, we get the Singleton instance and then invoke the closeDriver() method.

 
4.10 Introduction to Tags in TestRunner
 
We might have a collection of multiple scenarios in one Feature file and we also may have multiple Feature files as well. Suppose, we are doing Smoke, Regression, and FilterTest and want to group our scenarios under these, then we have the option of running each group separately. This can be achieved with the help of tags. Tags are written in the Feature file with the syntax shown as follows:
 
@Smoke
 
Similarly, if we wish to run test cases corresponding to the @Smoke tag, we need to mention this tag in the Test Runner in Cucumber options as indicated shown as follows:
 
@CucumberOptions(features = {"src/test/resources/featurefiles"}, glue = {"stepdefinitions"}, plugin = {
"pretty", "html:target/cucumber"}, tags =
 
Consider the example of a Feature file
 
#Sample Feature to show tags and tag inheritance
@FunctionalSuite
Feature: Title of your feature
I want to use this template for my feature file
 
@Smoke
Scenario: Smoke Test 1
Given I want to execute "Smoke Test 1" test
 
@FilterTest
Scenario: Filter Test 1
Given I want to execute "Filter Test 1" test
 
@Regression
Scenario: Regression Test 1
Given I want to execute "Regression Test 1" test
 
@Smoke @FilterTest
Scenario: Smoke/Filter Test 1
Given I want to execute "Smoke/Filter Test 1" test
 
@Smoke @Regression
Scenario: Smoke/Regression Test 1
Given I want to execute "Smoke/Regression" test
 
@Regression @FilterTest
Scenario: Regression/Filter Test 1
Given I want to execute "Regression/Filter Test 1" test
Scenario: Generic Test 1
Given I want to execute "Generic" test
 
The corresponding step definition is shown as follows:
 
public class BPBSD_4 {
@Given("^I want to execute \"([^\"]*)\" test$")
public void i_want_to_execute_test(String type) throws Throwable {
// Write code here that turns the phrase above into concrete actions
System.out.println("This test is of type: "+type);
}
}
 
If the TestRunner is executed with = then three scenarios get executed as shown in the following screenshot:
 
 
Figure 4.3: Tag execution
 
Next, we will see how to club two tags so that scenarios which have either of the tags get executed.

 
4.11 Designing Test Suites with the help of tags
 
In this section, we will see how to create test suites where we want to execute test cases corresponding to multiple tags. 5.1 Understanding the Page Object Design Pattern
 
The Page Object Design Pattern is a popular design pattern in test automation which is used for enhanced test maintenance and reduced code duplication. A page object is a Java class or any other OOP language class that represents a page of our AUT. The test classes which in our case will be the Step Definitions make use of the methods of this page object class whenever an action has to be performed on a page. The advantage of having such a structure is that if the UI changes for a particular page, there is no need of changing the tests. Only the Page Object classes undergo change. Hence, all changes required for the new UI are located in one place.
 
The Page Object Design Pattern has the following advantages:
  
There is a clear separation between test code and page-specific code such as locators and the methods that operate on those locators.
 
Since the locators are maintained in the Page Object class, the tests are clean with no locators scattered in them.
 
Now that we know what a Page Object Design pattern is, let’s take a look at the Page Object Model.

 
5.2 What is the Page Object Model?
 
The Page Object Model is derived from the Page Object Design pattern. Here, we will design a class for each page. This will be a Java class in our case. Let’s see the Login screen as shown in the following screenshot. We will consider this page and see a code snippet.
 
Click on the tab to navigate to the Login Page:
 
 
Figure 5.1: The Landing Page
 
We create a class called LandingPage.java:
 
package pageobjects;
package pageobjects;
import org.openqa.selenium.By;
import singletondriver.SingletonDriver;
public class LandingPage extends AbstractBasePage{
By btnLogin = By.xpath("//a[@href='https://ui.freecrm.com']");
public void clickLogin() {
SingletonDriver.getInstance().getDrvr().findElement(btnLogin).click();
}
 
@Override
public void setPageTitle(String pageTitle) {
this.pageTitle=pageTitle;
}
 
@Override
public String getPageTitle() {
return this.pageTitle;
}
}
 
In the preceding code, we have made use of the By class to create a locator for the Login button highlighted above. We use this locator in our method to perform the click action. Thus, everything related to this landing page will be present in the Landing page class.
 
In the Step Definition, we will simply create an object of the LandingPage class and invoke the clickLogin() method on it.
 
Since we made use of BY class above, let's dive deeper into the BY class.

 
5.3 Introducing the BY class
 
In order to locate elements, we make use of the BY class in Selenium. The BY class is an abstract class and has 8 static methods along with 8 inner classes. The 8 static methods help us locate elements based on ID, cssSelector, name, link text, class name, tag name, partial link text. and xpath. In section we saw the use of xpath to locate the Login button.
 
We will see a code skeleton for the BY class as follows:
 
public abstract class By {
public static By id(String id);
public static By cssSelector(String css);
public static By name(String name);
public static By linkText(String text);
public static By className(String className);
public static By tagName(String tagName);
public static By partialLinkText(String partialLinkText);
public static By xpath(String xpath);
public static class ById extends By {
WebElement findElement(By by);
List findElements(By by);
}
}

Let’s design a Login Scenario for our Page Object Model.

 
5.4 Designing a login scenario
 
In order to work with the automation of functional scenarios, we need to design a scenario for the Cucumber test execution. We will design a scenario in which we open a browser window, navigate to the www.freecrm.com website and click on the Login button. With this, we will navigate to the Login Page. We enter the username and password and click on the Login button on this page. After a successful login, we will verify the username displayed on top. The text to be verified is passed through the Feature file.
 
We need to perform the following steps:
  
Open the browser.
 
Navigate to the website
 
Click on the Login button.
 
Enter the UserName.
 
Enter the Password.
 
Click on the Login button.
 
Verify the User Name on top.
 
Close the browser.
 
Let’s take a look at our Feature file:
 
 
Figure 5.2: The Login Scenario
 
We have four pages to design. So let’s go step by step and as the first step, let’s design the Abstract Base Page Object which will serve to be a parent class for all other Page Objects.

 
5.5 Creating the Page Objects
 
In this section, we will learn how to create the three page objects starting with the parent of all Page Objects, which is the Abstract Base Page.

 
5.5.1 Creating the Abstract Base Page
 
We will create an abstract Base Page class that will serve as a base class of all Page Object classes. Right now, this page contains concrete methods for opening the browser and navigating to a URL. It also has abstract methods for setting and getting the Page Title. The Abstract Base Page class will have the openBrowser(String, String, String) and navigateURL() methods which are the two concrete methods. The URL is picked up from the GLOBAL_DATA class. The entry in the GLOBAL_DATA class is shown as follows:
 
public static final String URL="http://freecrm.co.in";
 
The AbstractBasePage class is shown as follows:
 
package pageobjects;
 
import constants.GLOBAL_DATA;
import singletondriver.SingletonDriver;
 
public abstract class AbstractBasePage {
protected String pageTitle;
public void navigateURL() {
SingletonDriver.getInstance().getDrvr().navigate().to(GLOBAL_DATA.URL);
}
 
public void openBrowser(String browserName, String platform, String gridSetting) {
try {
SingletonDriver.getInstance().setDrvr(browserName, platform, gridSetting, null);
} catch (Exception e) {
// TODO Auto-generated catch block
e.printStackTrace();
}
}
 
public abstract void setPageTitle(String pageTitle);
public abstract String getPageTitle();
}
 
Next, we will make use of inheritance and create three Page Objects, namely, LandingPage, LoginPage, and Homepage which extend this abstract class. Since our Page objects are concrete classes, we have to provide a method body for the two methods setPageTitle(String pageTitle) and Since we have the SingletonDriver already set up, we make use of it to create an instance of the Chrome Driver and navigate to the http://freecrm.co.in website. The navigateURL method lands us on the Landing page so that we can use it to click on the Login button that is in the Landing page.
 
Let’s design the Landing page next.

 
5.5.2 Creating the Landing Page
 
The Landing page is the one that loads when the browser is opened and navigation happens to Our only task on this page is to click on the Login button and land us on the Login Page. Let’s see how we can implement the Landing Page.
 
The Landing page extends the Abstract Base Page as follows:
 
package pageobjects;
import org.openqa.selenium.By;
import singletondriver.SingletonDriver;
public class LandingPage extends AbstractBasePage{
By btnLogin = By.xpath("//a[@href='https://ui.freecrm.com']");
public void clickLogin() {
SingletonDriver.getInstance().getDrvr().findElement(btnLogin).click();
}
 
@Override
public void setPageTitle(String pageTitle) {
this.pageTitle=pageTitle;
}
 
@Override
public String getPageTitle() {
return this.pageTitle;
}
}
 
We created a By locator for the Login button using xpath. We have a clickLogin() method that clicks the Login button and lands us on the LoginPage so that it can be used further. We have also implemented the abstracts methods from the Abstract Base Page, namely, setPageTitle(String) and
 
Now that we are on the let’s see how we can implement the LoginPage class.

 
5.5.3 Creating the login page
 
The LoginPage class has three WebElements to work with, namely, UserName textbox, Password textbox, and Login button. By clicking on the Login button, the user can navigate to the HomePage so that we can extract and verify the User Name displayed on top.
 
The Login page also extends the Abstract Base Page as follows:
 
package pageobjects;
import org.openqa.selenium.By;
import singletondriver.SingletonDriver;
public class LoginPage extends AbstractBasePage{
By email = By.name("email");
By password = By.name("password");
By btnLogin = By.xpath("//div[text()='Login']");
public void enterUserName(String userName) {
SingletonDriver.getInstance().getDrvr().findElement(email).sendKeys(userName);
}
public void enterPassword(String passwordtxt) {
SingletonDriver.getInstance().getDrvr().findElement(password).sendKeys(passwordtxt);
}
public void clickLogin() {
SingletonDriver.getInstance().getDrvr().findElement(btnLogin).click();
}
 
@Override
public void setPageTitle(String pageTitle) {
this.pageTitle = pageTitle;
}
 
@Override
public String getPageTitle() {
return this.pageTitle;
}
}
 
Now we are on the HomePage and we are in the final phase of verification of the UserName on the top panel. Let’s see the Homepage.java next.

 
5.5.4 Creating the Home Page
 
Now that we are on the Homepage, we make use of the getText() method to capture the text present for the UserName on the top panel. The procedure remains the same. We will create a variable of type ‘By’ for the UserName span. We also have the Logout functionality scripted in this class since the Logout appears on the HomePage after Logging In. Logout is a two-step process where the Logout icon is clicked first followed by clicking of the link. We can quit the browser after this. All this code has been kept in the logOut() method which is annotated with @After which ensures that this is run after every Feature.
 
The Homepage page object verifies the Username on the top of the page which is shown as follows:
 
package pageobjects;
 
import org.openqa.selenium.By;
import org.testng.Assert;
 
import cucumber.api.java.After;
import singletondriver.SingletonDriver;
 
public class Homepage extends AbstractBasePage{
By userDisplay = By.xpath("//span[@class='user-display']");
By logOutDiv = By.xpath("//div[@role='listbox']");
By logOutSpan = By.xpath("//span[text()='Log Out']");
public void verifyUser(String userDisplayText) {
System.out.println(SingletonDriver.getInstance().getDrvr().findElement(userDisplay).getText());
Assert.assertEquals(SingletonDriver.getInstance().getDrvr().findElement(userDisplay).getText(), userDisplayText);
}
 
@After
public void logOut() {
SingletonDriver.getInstance().getDrvr().findElement(logOutDiv).click();
SingletonDriver.getInstance().getDrvr().findElement(logOutSpan).click();
SingletonDriver.getInstance().getDrvr().close();
SingletonDriver.getInstance().getDrvr().quit();
}
 
@Override
public void setPageTitle(String title) {
this.pageTitle=pageTitle;
}
 
@Override
public String getPageTitle() {
return this.pageTitle;
}
}
 
Let’s understand the Step Definitions next.

 
5.6 Step definitions for the pages
 
In section we designed the three-page objects along with the Abstract Base Page. We have segregated our Step Definitions in three separate Java classes. Let’s see each Java class.

 
5.6.1 Landing Page Step definition
 
Let’s take a look at the Landing page step definitions. The first thing we do in this Step Definition is to create an object of the LandingPage. Using this object, we open a Chrome browser, navigate to the URL, and click on the Login button. Notice that the methods for opening a browser and navigating to the URL are present in the AbstractBasePage and not in the landing page, but since we have extended the Abstract Base Page for all our page objects, we can use the LandingPage object to invoke methods in the Abstract Base Page.
 
The LandingStepDef Step Definition that makes use of the LandingPage page object is shown as follows:
 
package stepdefinitions;
 
import constants.GLOBAL_DATA;
import cucumber.api.java.en.Given;
import cucumber.api.java.en.When;
import pageobjects.LandingPage;
 
public class LandingStepDef {
LandingPage = new LandingPage();
@Given("^I open the \"([^\"]*)\" browser on \"([^\"]*)\" and \"([^\"]*)\"$")
public void i_open_the_browser_on_and(String browser, String platform, String gridSetting) throws Throwable {
landingPage.openBrowser(browser, platform, gridSetting);
}
 
@When("^User navigates to the landing page$")
public void user_navigates_to_the_landing_page() throws Throwable {
landingPage.navigateURL();
}
 
@When("^clicks the Login button on the landing page$")
public void clicks_the_Login_button_on_the_landing_page() throws Throwable {
landingPage.clickLogin();
}
}
 
Now that we have navigated to the Login Page, let’s move on to the Login Page Step Definition.

 
5.6.2 Login Page Step Definition
 
Next in our list is the design of the Login Page Step Definition. Here, our task is to enter the email, password, and then click on the Login button. The code for the Login Page Step Definition is shown below. It basically has the same structure as the Landing Page Step Definition. We create an object of the LoginPage and then we enter the UserName, Password, and then click on the Login button using this object.
 
LoginStepDef makes use of the LoginPage page object as follows:
 
package stepdefinitions;
 
import cucumber.api.java.en.And;
import cucumber.api.java.en.When;
import pageobjects.LoginPage;
 
public class LoginStepDef {
LoginPage = new LoginPage();
@When("^User enters \"(.*?)\" as username$")
public void user_enters_admin_as_username(String userName) throws Throwable {
System.out.println("UserName is: "+userName);
loginPage.enterUserName(userName);
}
 
@And("^User enters \"(.*?)\" as password$")
public void user_enters_admin_as_password(String password) throws Throwable {
System.out.println("Password is: "+password);
loginPage.enterPassword(password);
}
 
@And("^User clicks the Login button$")
public void user_clicks_the_Login_button() throws Throwable {
System.out.println("Login button clicked");
loginPage.clickLogin();
}
}
 
Finally, we move to the Homepage step definition.

 
5.6.3 Home Page step definition
 
The Home Page step definition has a similar code structure to the landing page step definition and login page step definition. The code listing is given as follows:
