6.1 Understanding the Page Factory Design pattern
 
The Page Factory Design pattern is an extension to the Page Object Design pattern but is much more advanced. The creation of Page Objects is simplified by using the Page Factory pattern. The elements in the Page Objects can be initialized using the static method of the PageFactory class which is The PageFactory.initElements() static method takes two arguments, namely, the driver instance and the class type, and it returns a Page Object with its variables/fields which are initialized. The locators and the code using those locators can be in the same or different class. Generally, a different class is preferable.
 
The Page Factory Design pattern has the following advantages:
  
The WebElements of a web page are initialized at one go.
 
Since the locators are maintained in the Page Object class, the tests are clean with no locators scattered in them.
 
Now that we know what a Page Factory Design pattern is, let’s take a look at the PageFactory class.

 
6.2 Learning about the PageFactory class
 
The WebDriver library provides us with the PageFactory class so that we can create our Page Objects with ease. This ease of creating Page Objects is due to the annotations provided by the PageFactory class. WebElements can be pre-defined in the class and the PageFactory transforms the WebElements into Proxied objects where the Java proxy class is utilized. When the time comes to make use of these WebElements, the annotations provided by the PageFactory class transform the proxy objects in WebElements so that the WebElements can be used. A two-step process needs to be used:
  
Annotate the variables that we need to use (proxy) in our code.
 
Initialize the proxied elements with the initElements() method before using them.
 
Let’s first understand how to annotate the variables that we need to proxy.

 
6.3 Introducing the @FindBy, @FindBys, and @FindAll annotations
 
Let us see the various annotations that Cucumber provides. We will look at three annotations, namely, @FindBys, and Let’s start with the @FindBy annotation.

 
6.3.1 The @FindBy annotation
 
@FindBy is an annotation which specifies the Object Location strategy for a single WebElement or list of WebElements. The @FindBy annotation is used to find one or more WebElements using single search criteria. If we are sure that our search criteria will return a single WebElement, then we can use the annotation as follows:
 
@FindBy(how=How.XPATH,using="//a[@href='https://ui.freecrm.com']")
public WebElement btnLogin;
 
Here, the location strategy is specified using the XPATH strategy from the HOW enum. Here, we will find the WebElement with XPath //a[@href='https://ui.freecrm.com'] and assign it to the WebElement
 
If we are not sure about the number of WebElements returned by the search criteria, use a List instead of a single WebElement as follows:
 
@FindBy(how=How.CLASS_NAME,using="dummyclass")
public List txtBoxes;
 
Here, the location strategy is specified using the CLASS_NAME strategy from the HOW enum. Here, we will find the WebElement with Class Name dummyclass and assign it to a list of WebElements txtBoxes. We then need additional code to iterate through this list of WebElements.
 
Let’s next take a look at the @FindBys annotation.

 
6.3.2 The @FindBys annotation
 
When we need to find WebElements that match all of the given criteria, then in such a case @FindBys is used. More than single search criteria can be specified as follows:
 
@FindBys({
@FindBy(how = How.ID, using = "dummyid"),
@FindBy(how = How.NAME, using = "dummyname")
})
private List bothMatching;
 
In the preceding example, the list of WebElements will include WebElements which have the ID as and NAME as
 
Let’s see the @FindAll annotation next.

 
6.3.3 The @FindAll annotation
 
When we need to find WebElements that match at least one of the given criteria, then in such a case, @FindAll is used. More than single search criteria can be specified as follows:
 
@FindAll({
@FindBy(how = How.ID, using = "dummyid"),
@FindBy(how = How.NAME, using = "dummyname")
})
private List atleastOneMatching;
 
In the preceding example, the list of WebElements will include WebElements which have the ID as or NAME as
 
Let’s see how to initialize the proxied elements with the initElements() method before using them in the code.

 
6.4 Understanding the initElements method
 
In this section, we will take a look at step two of section 6.2 which is about initializing the proxied elements. The PageFactory class provides us with a static initElements method which can be used for this purpose. There are three overloaded versions of this method which are as follows:
  
public static void initElements(WebDriver driver, java.lang.Object page)
 
This is the basic version which takes a WebDriver and page class as arguments.
 
public static void initElements(ElementLocatorFactory factory, java.lang.Object page)
 
This version takes a ElementLocatorFactory that is used to provide a mechanism for finding elements and page class as arguments.
 
public static void initElements(FieldDecorator field, java.lang.Object page)
 
This version takes a FieldDecorator that is used to decorate each of the fields.
 
We will see the annotations and the initElements() method in action when we explore the sample scenario.

 
6.5 Designing the Page Factory framework
 
We will use a similar structure as the Page Object Model. We will create two additional packages under src/main/java, namely, where the ‘pf’ at the end stands for Page Factory and locators, which will have Java classes with the @FindBy annotation. Public WebElements will be maintained in these classes so that they are accessible for the Java classes that utilize these variables. All Page Objects will inherit an AbstractBasePagePF class. This class will have two concrete methods, openBrowser(String, String, String) and It will also have two abstract methods for getting and setting the Page Title. Since we have three pages to work with, we will have three page objects and three step definitions.
 
The Page Factory framework designed in such a manner will help splitting the work of creating the Object Repository [Classes for Locators] and Page Objects and can be done independently of each other without dependencies involved.

 
6.6 Designing a Login scenario
 
We will start with a simple scenario as follows:
  
Open the browser.
 
Navigate to the website
 
Click on the Login button.
 
Enter UserName.
 
Enter Password.
 
Click on the Login button.
 
Verify the User Name on top of page.
 
Close the browser.
 
Let’s take a look at our Feature file as shown in the following screenshot:
 
 
Figure 6.1: Login Scenario
 
We have three pages for the locators to design. So let’s go step by step and as the first step, let’s design the locators for the Landing Page, Login Page, and Home Page which will be used by their respective Page Objects.

 
6.7 Creating the Page Locators using @FindBy
 
In this section, we will create the locator classes for the Landing Page, Login Page, and Home Page. This class will have locators designed as per the Page Factory style with the @FindBy annotation.
 
Let's start with the locators for the Landing Page.

 
6.7.1 Creating the Landing Page Locators
 
The landing page has the Login button that needs to be clicked to open the Login page. Here is the content of the LandingPageLocators.java that has one WebElement defined with the @FindBy annotation:
 
package locators;
 
import org.openqa.selenium.WebElement;
import org.openqa.selenium.support.FindBy;
import org.openqa.selenium.support.How;
 
public class LandingPageLocators {
@FindBy(how=How.XPATH,using="//a[@href='https://ui.freecrm.com']")
public WebElement btnLogin;
}
 
This is a straightforward class with just one WebElement for the Login button. We are locating the Login button using the XPath strategy.

 
6.7.2 Creating the Login Page locators
 
The login page has the email address and password text boxes and the Login button. Here is the content of the LoginPageLocators.java that has three WebElements defined with the @FindBy annotation:
 
package locators;
 
import org.openqa.selenium.WebElement;
import org.openqa.selenium.support.FindBy;
import org.openqa.selenium.support.How;
 
public class LoginPageLocators {
@FindBy(name="email")
public WebElement email;
 
@FindBy(name="password")
public WebElement password;
 
@FindBy(how=How.XPATH,using="//div[text()='Login']")
public WebElement btnLogin;
}
 
This class finds elements based on the name as well as the X-Path Strategy.

 
6.7.3 Creating the Home Page locators
 
The Home page has the User Name display on top that needs to be verified. In addition to this, it also has the LogOut Div and LogOut span. Here is the content of the HomePageLocators.java that has three WebElements defined with the @FindBy annotation:
 
package locators;
 
import org.openqa.selenium.WebElement;
import org.openqa.selenium.support.FindBy;
import org.openqa.selenium.support.How;
 
public class HomepageLocators {
 
@FindBy(how=How.XPATH,using="//span[@class='user-display']")
public WebElement userDisplay;
 
@FindBy(how=How.XPATH,using="//div[@role='listbox']")
public WebElement logOutDiv;
 
@FindBy(how=How.XPATH,using="//span[text()='Log Out']")
public WebElement logOutSpan;
}
 
This class finds elements based on the X-Path Strategy. Now that we have created individual classes for the locators, let’s go ahead and design our Page Objects. There are four classes involved: The Abstract Base Page, Landing Page Object, Login Page Object, and Home Page object.

 
6.8 Creating the Page Objects
 
In this section, we will learn how to create the three page objects starting with the parent of all Page Objects, which is the Abstract Base Page.

 
6.8.1 Creating the Abstract Base Page
 
We will create an abstract Base Page class that will serve as a base class of all Page Object classes. Right now, this page contains concrete methods for opening the browser and navigating to a URL. It also has abstract methods for setting and getting the Page Title. The Abstract Base Page class will have the openBrowser(String, String, String) and navigateURL() methods which are the two concrete methods. The URL is picked up from the GLOBAL_DATA class. The entry in the GLOBAL_DATA class is as follows:
 
public static final String URL="http://freecrm.co.in";
 
The AbstractBasePage class is shown as follows:
 
package pageobjectspf;
 
import constants.GLOBAL_DATA;
import pageobjectspf.LandingPagePF;
import singletondriver.SingletonDriver;
 
public abstract class AbstractBasePagePF {
protected String pageTitle;
 
public LandingPagePF navigateURL() {
SingletonDriver.getInstance().getDrvr().navigate().to(GLOBAL_DATA.URL);
return new LandingPagePF();
}
 
public void openBrowser(String browserName, String platform, String gridSetting) {
try {
SingletonDriver.getInstance().setDrvr(browserName, platform, gridSetting, null);
} catch (Exception e) {
// TODO Auto-generated catch block
e.printStackTrace();
}
}
public abstract void setPageTitle(String pageTitle);
public abstract String getPageTitle();
}
 
Note that the navigateURL returns an object of the LandingPage when the control is sent back to the child class LandingPage that inherits the AbstractBasePagePF class. When we see the Step Definitions in the later section, we will see how to get a hold of this returned object to do actions on the Landing Page.
 
Next, we will make use of inheritance and create three Page Objects, namely, LandingPage, LoginPage, and Homepage which extend this abstract class. Since our Page objects are concrete classes, we have to provide a method body for the two methods setPageTitle(String pageTitle) and Since we have the SingletonDriver already set up, we make use of it to create an instance of the Chrome Driver and navigate to the http://freecrm.co.in website. The navigateURL method lands us on the Landing page so that we can use it to click on the Login button that is in the Landing page.
 
Let’s design the Landing page next.

 
6.8.2 Creating the Landing Page
 
The Landing page is the one which loads when the browser is opened and navigation happens in Our only task on this page is to click on the Login button and land on the Login Page. Let’s see how we have implemented the Landing Page. The Landing page extends the Abstract Base Page. We will use the concept of composition and create an object of the LandingPageLocators class inside the LandingPagePF page object. Inside the constructor, we will instantiate the landingPageLocators object and initialize all WebElements at one go using the initElements method which takes as argument the driver instance and the LandingPageLocators object.
 
package pageobjectspf;
 
import org.openqa.selenium.support.PageFactory;
import locators.LandingPageLocators;
import singletondriver.SingletonDriver;
 
public class LandingPagePF extends AbstractBasePagePF{
LandingPageLocators;
public LandingPagePF() {
super();
landingpageLocators = new LandingPageLocators();
PageFactory.initElements(SingletonDriver.getInstance().getDrvr(), landingpageLocators);
System.out.println("After init");
}
public void clickLogin() {
System.out.println("Before click"+this.landingpageLocators.btnLogin.getText());
landingpageLocators.btnLogin.click();
System.out.println("After click");
}
 
@Override
public void setPageTitle(String pageTitle) {
this.pageTitle=pageTitle;
}
 
@Override
public String getPageTitle() {
return this.pageTitle;
}
}
 
We have a clickLogin() method that clicks the Login button and lands us on LoginPage so that it can be used further. We have also implemented the abstracts methods from the Abstract Base Page, namely, setPageTitle(String) and
 
Now that we are on the LoginPage, let’s see how we can implement the LoginPage class.

 
6.8.3 Creating the Login page
 
The LoginPage class has three WebElements to work with, namely, UserName textbox, Password textbox, and Login button. After clicking on the Login button, the user needs to navigate to the HomePage so that we can extract and verify the User Name displayed on the top:
 
package pageobjectspf;
 
import org.openqa.selenium.support.PageFactory;
import locators.LoginPageLocators;
import singletondriver.SingletonDriver;
 
public class LoginPagePF extends AbstractBasePagePF{
LoginPageLocators;
public LoginPagePF() {
super();
loginpageLocators = new LoginPageLocators();
PageFactory.initElements(SingletonDriver.getInstance().getDrvr(), loginpageLocators);
}
 
public void enterUserName(String userName) {
loginpageLocators.email.sendKeys(userName);
}
public void enterPassword(String passwordtxt) {
loginpageLocators.password.sendKeys(passwordtxt);
}
public void clickLogin() {
loginpageLocators.btnLogin.click();
}
 
@Override
public void setPageTitle(String pageTitle) {
this.pageTitle = pageTitle;
}
 
@Override
public String getPageTitle() {
return this.pageTitle;
}
}
 
Now we are on the HomePage and we are in the final phase of verification of the UserName on the top panel. Let’s see the Homepage.java next.

 
6.8.4 Creating the Home page
 
Now that we are on the Homepage, we will make use of the getText() method to capture the text present for UserName on the top panel. The procedure remains the same. We have the Logout functionality scripted in this class since the Logout appears on the HomePage after logging in. Logout is a two-step process where the Logout icon is clicked first followed by clicking on the ‘Log out’ link. We will quit the browser after this. All this code has been kept in the logOut() method. Logout happens after each Feature finishes execution as the logOut() method is annotated with the @After annotation.
  
Note: We can also keep the method annotated with the @After annotation in a different class based on requirements.
  
The code listing is given as follows:
 
package pageobjectspf;
 
import org.openqa.selenium.support.PageFactory;
import org.testng.Assert;
 
import locators.HomepageLocators;
import singletondriver.SingletonDriver;
 
public class HomepagePF extends AbstractBasePagePF{
HomepageLocators;
public HomepagePF() {
super();
homepageLocators = new HomepageLocators();
PageFactory.initElements(SingletonDriver.getInstance().getDrvr(), homepageLocators);
}
 
public void verifyUser(String userDisplayText) {
System.out.println(homepageLocators.userDisplay.getText());
Assert.assertEquals(homepageLocators.userDisplay.getText(), userDisplayText);
}
 
@After
public void logOut() {
homepageLocators.logOutDiv.click();
homepageLocators.logOutSpan.click();
SingletonDriver.getInstance().getDrvr().close();
SingletonDriver.getInstance().getDrvr().quit();
}
 
@Override
public void setPageTitle(String title) {
this.pageTitle=pageTitle;
}
 
@Override
public String getPageTitle() {
return this.pageTitle;
}
}
 
With this, we are done with creating the Abstract Base page along with the three page objects for the Landing Page, Login Page, and Home Page.
 
Let’s understand the Step definitions next.

 
6.9 Step definitions for the pages
 
In section 6.8, we designed the three page objects along with the Abstract Base Page. We have segregated our Step Definitions in three separate java classes. Let’s see each Java class.

 
6.9.1 Landing page step definition
 
Let’s take a look at the Landing page step definitions. The first thing we do in this Step Definition is to create an object of the LandingPage. Using this object, we will open a Chrome browser, navigate to the URL, and click on the Login button. Notice that the methods for opening a browser and navigating to the URL are present in the AbstractBasePage and not in the landing page but since we have extended the Abstract Base Page for all our page objects, we can use the LandingPage object to invoke methods in the Abstract Base Page. Also, note that we are capturing the returned LandingPage object from the navigateURL() method and making use of it to do the click operation of the Login button on the Landing page. The code is as follows:
 
package stepdefinitions;
 
import constants.GLOBAL_DATA;
import cucumber.api.java.en.Given;
import cucumber.api.java.en.When;
import pageobjects.LandingPage;
import pageobjectspf.LandingPagePF;
 
public class LandingStepDefPF {
LandingPagePF landingPagePF = new LandingPagePF();
@Given("^The user opens the \"([^\"]*)\" browser on \"([^\"]*)\" and \"([^\"]*)\"$")
public void i_open_the_browser_on_and(String browser, String platform, String gridSetting) throws Throwable {
landingPagePF.openBrowser(browser, platform, gridSetting);
}
 
@When("^The user navigates to the landing page$")
public void user_navigates_to_the_landing_page() throws Throwable {
landingPagePF = landingPagePF.navigateURL();
}
 
@When("^The user clicks the Login button on the landing page$")
public void The_user_clicks_the_Login_button_on_the_landing_page() throws Throwable {
landingPagePF.clickLogin();
}
}
 
Now that we have navigated to the Login page, let’s move on to the Login Page Step Definition.

 
6.9.2 Login page step definition
 
Next in our list is the design of the Login Page Step Definition. Here, our task is to enter the email, password, and then click on the Login button. The code for the Login Page Step Definition is shown as follows. It basically has the same structure as the Landing Page Step Definition. We created an object of the LoginPage and then we entered the Password, and then clicked on the Login button using this object. The code is as follows:
 
package stepdefinitions;
 
import cucumber.api.java.en.And;
import cucumber.api.java.en.When;
import pageobjects.LoginPage;
import pageobjectspf.LoginPagePF;
 
public class LoginStepDefPF {
LoginPagePF loginPagePF = new LoginPagePF();
@When("^The user enters \"(.*?)\" as username$")

Finally, we move on to the Homepage Step Definition.

 
6.9.3 Home page step definition
 
The Home Page step definition has a similar code structure to the Landing Page Step Definition and Login Page Step Definition. We created an object of the HomePage and used it to fetch the text of the The code listing is given as follows:

Finally, we will see an annotation that can be useful to speed up the test execution by caching the Web Elements. This annotation is the @CacheLookup annotation used in the Step Definitions.

 
6.10 Understanding the @CacheLookup annotation
 
The @FindBy annotation does the following when used in a Step Definition:
  
Navigates to the Document Object Model.
 
Searches for the element.
 
Initializes the element.
 
The element is ready for operations such as click().
 
There are many operations that are performed on WebElements and in a big project, there can be hundreds or even thousands of such WebElements. This increases the test execution time and reduces productivity.
 
To tackle this situation, Cucumber provides us with the @CacheLookup annotation. This annotation, when applied over a WebElement, instructs Selenium to maintain this WebElement in the Cache. Every Time afterwards, when an operation is performed on that particular WebElement, the element is picked from the Cache, thus saving the execution time.
 
The way we apply this annotation in the Page Object classes is shown as follows:
 
@CacheLookup
@FindBy(how=How.XPATH,using="//div[@role='listbox']")
public WebElement logOutDiv;
 
We will use @CacheLookup in all our Page Objects as we proceed to the remaining chapters.

7.1 Introduction to the TestNG framework
 
TestNG is a test automation framework where NG represents the next generation.TestNG is a combination of JUnit (in Java) and NUnit (in C#). It is frequently used for unit, functional, integration, and end-to-end testing. TestNG has become very popular in the test automation area within a short time and has become one of the most widely used testing frameworks among developers (both application and test automation developers). It mainly uses annotations in Java to configure and write test methods.
 
TestNG was introduced by Cedric Beust. He developed it to overcome shortcomings in JUnit. A few of the features of TestNG are as follows:
  
Additional before and after annotations like @AfterTest
 
@AfterClass
 
Grouping test methods by creating TestNG groups
 
Incorporating dependencies using dependsOn
 
Executing tests in parallel
 
Basic test execution reporting
 
TestNG is a testing framework which is written in Java and can be used with Java and also with Java-related languages such as Groovy. In TestNG, suites and tests are configured through the use of XML files. By default, the name of this file is testng.xml, but it can be given another name if need be.
 
TestNG enables us to do test configuration through XML files and allows us to include (or exclude) respective packages, classes, and methods in the test suite. It also allows users to group test methods into particular named groups, which can be included or excluded as part of the test execution.
 
Parameterization of test methods is easy using TestNG, and it also provides the facility of creating data-driven tests.
 
TestNG has exposed its API, which has made it easy to add custom functionalities or extensions if required.

7.4 Various annotations in TestNG
 
Let’s take a look at the various annotations that we have used in our Test Runner class:
  
@BeforeClass
 
The method annotated with this annotation gets executed before any test method in the current class.
 
@AfterClass
 
The method annotated with this annotation gets executed after all test methods in the current class have been invoked.
 
@Test
 
The method/methods annotated with this annotation gets executed as a part of the test.
 
@DataProvider
 
The method annotated with this annotation is useful for providing test data to the methods annotated as The data provider method itself has an annotation of and an optional name.

Apache Maven is a popular tool for automating software projects, mainly Java projects and is also used for building Selenium projects. Maven addresses two aspects of the software build process. It specifies how a software is built and also describes its dependencies. Maven uses convention over configuration for the build process. An XML file also known as pom.xml stands for Project Object describes the software project that is being built, its dependencies on other modules or components, directories, the build order, and necessary plugins. It comes with predefined targets to perform tasks, such as code compilation and packaging. Maven dynamically downloads Maven plugins and Java libraries from one or more online repositories, such as the Maven Central and stores them locally in the Local Repository.
 
Let’s take the first step towards Maven by downloading and installing it.

 
8.1 Downloading and extracting Maven
 
We will cover the Maven download process for Windows. The prerequisites for Maven installation are as follows:
  
Java should be installed [Preferably version 1.8]. Make sure the JDK is present.
 
The JAVA_HOME environment variable should be configured.
 
Path to the bin folder of Java should be configured in the path environment variable.
 
Navigate to http://maven.apache.org and download the zip file corresponding to the latest stable release. Extract it to a convenient location. Once extracted, the folder structure should include the folders mentioned as follows:
  
This contains the required files to run Maven on different platforms.
 
This contains the settings.xml file which can be used to configure certain Maven settings.
 
This contains the required jar files for Maven to start.
 
This contains the libraries used by Maven along with an ext folder which contains third-party extensions to change the default Maven implementation.
 
Once Maven is downloaded and extracted, we need to add a new environment variable and edit the Environment variable.

8.3 Understanding Maven local and central repositories
 
A repository in Maven is a physical directory that contains JAR files along with meta data about the JAR files. The meta data is in the form of POM files which has project information and other external dependencies that the JAR file has. There are two kinds of repositories, namely, Local and Central.
 
Let’s understand the difference between the two:
  
Local This resides on the developer’s machine in C:\Users\pinakin.chaubal\.m2\repository.
 
Central This is located at When a Maven build job is run, Maven tries to locate the dependency in the local repository and if it is unable to find the dependency in the local repository, the dependency gets downloaded from the Central Repository into the .m2 folder mentioned above.
 
When we learn about the POM XML file, we will see how to mention dependencies of the project along with the versions. Let’s learn a little about the build phases in Maven.

 
8.4 Learning about Maven build lifecycle phases and goals
 
Maven is based on the concept of a build lifecycle where the process of building and distributing a particular artifact is defined clearly. The person in charge of the project build has to know only a limited number of commands to run a Maven project and the POM file takes care of getting this done for us. There are three build lifecycles that are built in, namely, default, clean, and site. A brief description of the three build lifecycles is given as follows:
  
default This handles the project deployment.
 
clean This handles the project cleaning.
 
site This handles the project’s site documentation.
 
Each build lifecycle is defined by a different list of build phases. A build phase is nothing but a stage in the lifecycle. As an example, let’s consider the default lifecycle which comprises the following phases:
  
The project is validated for correctness and availability of necessary information.
 
This is used for compilation of the source code of the project.
 
The compiled source code is tested using a unit testing framework like TestNG or Junit.
 
The compiled code is packaged into a distributable format like JAR.
 
Checks are run on the results of integration tests to ensure quality of deliverables.
 
The package is installed in the local repository so that it can be used as a dependency for other projects locally.
 
This is done in the build environment where the final package is copied to the remote repository so that it can be used by other projects.
 
In our case, when we say ‘mvn test’, the validate and compile phases get executed before the test phase. The default lifecycle phases get executed in order, starting from validate and ending at the desired phase.
 
Let’s understand the concept of plugin goals.
 
A plugin goal represents a task which is fine grained than a build phase and contributes to the building and managing of a project. It may be bound to either zero or more build phases. A goal that is not bound to any build phase can be executed independently outside the build lifecycle through direct invocation.
 
Let’s take a look at the pom.xml in detail.

 
8.5 Understanding the pom.xml
 
In this section, we will understand what the pom.xml file is and what goes into it. POM stands for Project Object Model and the pom.xml is used for configurations of a Maven Project. The pom.xml file is based on a specific schema as indicated in the tag shown as follows:
 
xmlns="http://maven.apache.org/POM/4.0.0" xmlns:xsi="http://www.w3.org/2001/XMLSchema-instance" xsi:schemaLocation="http://maven.apache.org/POM/4.0.0 http://maven.apache.org/xsd/maven-4.0.0.xsd">
 
The version of the schema is indicated in the tag as follows:
 
4.0.0
 
The group ID is indicated by the groupId tag and it is a unique ID for the organization indicated as a reverse domain name as follows:
 
bpb.cucumber
 
The artifact ID indicates the name of the project as follows:
 
cucumberpom
 
The version tag relates to the specific instance of our project. ‘SNAPSHOT’ indicates that this is work in progress:
 
0.0.1-SNAPSHOT
 
The build tag specifies the plugins to be used in the project. In our case, we have two plugins specified in the POM.XML file, namely, the Maven Compiler Plugin and Maven Surefire plugin.
 
The dependencies tag specifies all the external dependencies in the form of JAR files required for the project. These dependencies are downloaded automatically when the pom file is saved.
 
That is all that is needed to know about the POM file as far as our framework is concerned. Let’s now learn about Maven profiles.

A portable build is one that works on different platforms and runtime environments. Profiles can be used to build the same project in a different manner depending on the platform and environment. dev
/path/to/tomcat/instance

Global profile defined in the settings.xml in the Maven home directory.
 
Per project profile defined in the pom file of the project.
 
Per user profile defined in the user settings in the .m2 folder under the User’s home folder.

8.9 Dependency management in Maven
 
One of the prominent features of Maven is managing the dependencies required by a particular project. A project always or most of the time depends on other executables or dependencies. The typical issues faced while using dependencies are related to the choice of dependencies, the versions, and the transitive dependencies (a dependency being dependent on other dependencies).
 
The way we specify dependencies in a pom file is by mentioning a tag inside the tag is shown as follows:
 
io.cucumber
cucumber-java
6.10.3
 
Here, we are mentioning the dependency for cucumber-java where the version is 1.2.4. Maven looks into the local repository first to see whether the jar with the specified version exists. If it does not exist, then it is downloaded from the Maven central repository to the local repository.

Logging in any automation framework is an important activity. It gives the test engineer information on what happened in the test execution since most of the time, tests get executed in off hours. Through logging, the engineer can figure out the line number and the module in case of failures in the test execution.
 
Let’s understand the Log4J framework which we will use for logging in test automation.

 
9.1 Understand the Log4J framework
 
Log4J is a logging framework written in Java that is used for generating logs during test execution.
 
Log4J is configurable through external configuration files which can be either xml or property files. In order to use Log4J, the log4J dependency should be added to the pom.xml as follows:
 
log4j
log4j
1.2.17
 
After including this dependency, right click on the project and select Maven | Update The required JAR files will be downloaded in the .m2 folder.
 
Log4J has three main components listed as follows:
  
This is used for capturing logging information.
 
This is used for redirecting logging information to various preferred destinations [like Console or File Systems].
 
This is used for formatting logging information in different styles.
 
Let’s understand the steps involved in using Log4J to log user-defined output statements in the code.

 
9.2 Create a generic class for logging
 
For logging information to the console and file, we will use a user-defined class. This will be a very simple class as follows.
 
Create a class called LoggerUtil.java in the package utils in src/main/java as follows:
 
package utils;
 
import org.apache.log4j.Logger;
import org.apache.log4j.PropertyConfigurator;
 
public class LoggerUtil {
private static boolean customRoot=false;
public static Logger getCustomLogger(Class mycls){
if(customRoot){
return Logger.getLogger(mycls);
}
PropertyConfigurator.configure("log4j.properties");
customRoot = true;
return Logger.getLogger(mycls);
}
}
 
The preceding LoggerUtil class defines a static Boolean variable called If the root logger for Log4J has been already created by any class in the framework, the logger for that class will be returned else a new logger gets created.
 
Let’s move to the log4j.properties file creation.

 
9.2.1 Create a log4j.properties file
 
Along with this class, we should have the log4j.properties file at the root of the project.
 
The contents of the log4j.properties is shown as follows:
 
# Define custom root logger with file appender. Level of the root logger is defined as INFO
log4j.rootLogger = INFO, FILE, stdout
 
# Define the FILE Appender, the threshhold, the layout and the
# conversion #pattern
# The logging levels are in the order ALL(Integer.MAX_VALUE)
# < #DEBUG(500) < #INFO(400) < WARN(300) < ERROR(200) <
# FATAL(100) < OFF(0). Since we #have kept the logging #level # at
# INFO here, all INFO,WARN,ERROR,FATAL messages #will be displayed.
# The DEBUG and #TRACE level messages are not displayed
 
log4j.appender.FILE=org.apache.log4j.FileAppender
log4j.appender.FILE.File=automationtest.out
log4j.appender.FILE.MaxFileSize=20MB
log4j.appender.FILE.MaxBackupIndex=5
log4j.appender.FILE.Append=true
log4j.appender.FILE.layout=org.apache.log4j.PatternLayout
log4j.appender.FILE.layout.ConversionPattern=%d{yyyy-MM-dd HH:MM:SS} %-5p %c{1}:%L - %m%n
log4j.appender.FILE.Threshold=INFO
 
# This will print log in console
log4j.appender.stdout=org.apache.log4j.ConsoleAppender
log4j.appender.stdout.Target=System.out
log4j.appender.stdout.layout=org.apache.log4j.PatternLayout
log4j.appender.stdout.layout.ConversionPattern=%d{yyyy-MM-dd HH:MM:SS} %-5p %c{1} :%L - %m%n
log4j.appender.stdout.Threshold=INFO
 
The log messages will be pushed to the automationtest.out file, which will be appended every. On reaching 20 MB, a new file gets created. The new file will be an archived version, and at the place where it shows the type, the version number will be listed. For example, the first file will be of type 1 and the second of type 2. When the version 2 file is created, the version 1 file data will be pushed to version 2, and the current version data will be pushed to version 1. The next thing worth mentioning is that there can be only five versions that can be created, as indicated by MaxBackupIndex. After the fifth version, once maxFileSize is reached, data will start flowing from the current version to version 1, from version 1 to version 2, version 2 to version 3, and so on. Data in version 5 that was originally there will be overwritten by data from version 4.
 
Another point to note is about the logging levels. Logging levels are used to categorize entries in log files. This categorization is done based on urgency. Using logging levels one can manage the information that is logged. There are 8 logging levels which are listed as follows:
  
This turns on all levels of logging.
 
This is used for debugging. Messages appear in log files once this level is set.
 
This is used to record messages about routine operations of the application.
 
This is used to indicate that an error exists in the system.
 
This indicates a serious problem that requires immediate attention.
 
This indicates a very serious problem which might result in a system crash if not addressed immediately.
 
This turns off logging.
 
This is introduced in version 1.2 and adds more information to DEBUG level logs.
 
Let’s see how we can invoke this custom logger from our page objects.

 
9.3 Invoke the custom logger from the page objects
 
In order to invoke the custom logger from the page objects, we need to get the logger for the respective class from the CustomLogger class and then use the info(String) method wherever required. Here is the sample code that has to be included in the page objects.
 
Perform the following steps:
  
Include the following line of code as the first line in the Page Object classes:
 
Logger logger = LoggerUtil.getCustomLogger(LoginPagePF.class);
 
Include logging statements wherever necessary in the code as follows:
 
public void enterUserName(String userName) {
logger.info("Entering username");
loginpageLocators.email.sendKeys(userName);
}

10.1 Understand the Maven Surefire plugin
 
The Surefire plugin is used during the test phase of the build lifecycle to execute the unit tests of an application. It generates reports in two different file formats for normal Java programs:
  
Plain text files (*.txt)
 
XML files (*.xml)
 
By default, these files are generated in ${basedir}/target/surefire-reports/
 
TEST-*.xml.
 
Let’s see how to use the Suite XML files for executing TestNG xml next.

 
10.2 Configure the pom for using the Surefire plugin
 
In order to use TestNG suite XML files such as the testng xml, a Surefire plugin with the configuration shown below should be added. This allows the flexible configuration of the tests to be run. Add the xml snippet to the pom.xml in the tags as follows:
 
org.apache.maven.plugins
maven-surefire-plugin
2.14.1
testng.xml
 
In the preceding configuration, the testng.xml should be at the same level as the The testng.xml file is specified within a tag.

Let’s start by understanding the tag of the Maven Surefire plugin which will help in the continuation of the test execution even if scenarios fail.

 
11.1 Understanding the tag
 
On occasions where there are hundreds of tests to be executed, we may want to continue execution even if few of the tests fail. The feature file design should be such that the tests are mutually independent of each other and can execute without a dependency on other feature files. The tag helps to ignore failures in the test execution and move to the next scenario. The scenario design should be such that each of the scenarios should be a complete one. If a scenario opens a browser window, then the same scenario should close the browser window so that the next scenario starts afresh without stale browser sessions.
 
The xml fragment from the POM xml is shown as follows:
 
org.apache.maven.plugins
maven-surefire-plugin
2.14.1
testng.xml
false
true
 
As shown in the preceding code, we will ignore test failures in our test execution so that all scenarios in all the feature files get executed and we get a consolidated output.

11.3 Capturing screenshots of failed scenario steps
 
A very common practice in test automation is capturing screenshots when a failure occurs. Selenium provides us with the TakesScreenshot interface and the getScreenshotAs() method. The TakesScreenshot interface is used for capturing the screenshot and storing it in a specified location. We will capture the screenshot of the entire page. After taking the screenshot, it needs to be stored somewhere at a convenient location. Cucumber provides the embed(byte[], String) method for embedding the screenshot directly into the Cucumber JVM report. The screenshot is stored in a byte array which is then passed to the embed method which places the screenshot in the Cucumber JVM report.
 
We will place the method for taking screenshots on failure in the method annotated with @After so that it runs at the end of the scenario. The After Hook is shown as follows:
 
package stepdefinitions;
 
import org.openqa.selenium.OutputType;
import org.openqa.selenium.TakesScreenshot;
 
import cucumber.api.Scenario;
import cucumber.api.java.After;
import locators.HomepageLocators;
import pageobjects.AbstractBasePage;
import singletondriver.SingletonDriver;
import utils.Assertions;
 
public class BPBSD_99 {
@After
public void tearDown(Scenario scenario) {
if (scenario.isFailed()) {
byte[] screenPrint = ((TakesScreenshot)SingletonDriver.getInstance().getDrvr()).getScreenshotAs(OutputType.BYTES);
scenario.embed(screenPrint, "image/png");
}
try {
if (!(SingletonDriver.getInstance().getSessId()==null)) {
SingletonDriver.getInstance().getDrvr().close();
SingletonDriver.getInstance().getDrvr().quit();
}
} catch (Exception e) {
e.printStackTrace();
}
}
}
 
We will take a look at the output when we verify the JVM report.

 
11.4 Modifying the Test Runner for Cucumber JVM reports
 
Till now we have been using a Test Runner with @DataProvider, and @AfterClass annotations. Now onwards, we will use a simpler version of the TestRunner as follows:
 
package testrunner;
 
import cucumber.api.CucumberOptions;
import cucumber.api.testng.AbstractTestNGCucumberTests;
 
@CucumberOptions(features = {"src/test/resources/featurefiles"}, glue = {"stepdefinitions"}, plugin = {
"pretty", "json:target/cucumber-reports/cucumber-test.json"}, tags = {"@Sanity1"})
public class BPBTR_2 extends AbstractTestNGCucumberTests {
}
 
We still extend the Runner class with AbstractTestNGCucumberTests in order to use TestNG. We also use the @CucumberOptions annotation that has the location of our feature file and step definitions. We will also specify the location of the json file that gets generated at the end of the execution. We have tags mentioned so that only feature files that have the tag as @Sanity1 get executed.
 
Those are the changes that need to be done in the Test Runner. Let’s go ahead and create test cases in the form of Feature files.

Let’s start by understanding what Extent reports are along with the Maven dependency.

 
12.1 Introduction to Extent reports
 
Extent reports offer several features (when compared to the built-in reports that are generated through Cucumber). These reports include pie chart generation, scenario-wise report generation, adding screenshots, and so on, for every failed scenario and a beautiful user interface that can be shared with all stakeholders of the project.

 
12.1.1 Advantages of Extent reports
 
There are several advantages provided by extent reports and few of them are discussed as follows:
  
HTML reports with pie chart representation, which is customizable
 
Displays the time taken for scenario execution
 
Multiple test case runs within a single suite can be tracked easily
 
It can be integrated with TestNG and JUnit frameworks quite easily

 
12.1.2 Components of Extent reports
 
We will use two classes of Extents reports:
  
ExtentReports class: This class is mainly used for starting reporters and building reports. There should be one ExtentReports instance for the entire JVM.
 
ExtentHtmlReporter class: This class creates a rich standalone HTML file. It provides several configuration options via the config() method.
 
We will create a Custom Reporter class for generating Extent reports. There will be a generic helper for capturing screenshots.
 
Let’s look at what dependencies are required for incorporating Extent reports.

12.3 Creating a class for generating Extent reports
 
We will create a class called to create our Extent reports. This class will have the methods shown as follows:
  
createCustomTest(Scenario, This method gets the scenario title and error message if the scenario has failed. It creates a test using the status of the scenario using the getStatus() method of the Scenario object. If the scenario has failed, it attaches a screenshot as well as prints the error message to the report.
 
The createCustomTest(Scenario, String) method is shown as follows:
 
public void createCustomTest(Scenario scenario,String screenshotFile)
throws IOException {
if (scenario!=null) {
String testName = getScenarioTitle(scenario);
String errMessage = fetchErrorMsg(scenario);
switch(scenario.getStatus().toUpperCase()) {
case "PASSED":
extentReports.createTest(testName).pass("passed");
break;
case "FAILED":
System.out.println("in failed");
extentReports.createTest(testName).fail(errMessage).a
ddScreenCaptureFromPath(screenshotFile);
break;
default:
extentReports.createTest(testName).fail("skipped");
}
}
}
 
We have used the fetchErrorMsg(Scenario) to get the error message attached to the scenario, and we need access to the stepResults ArrayList as follows:
 
 
Figure 12.1: The private stepResults arrayList
 
The following step 7 of a feature file has failed. We need to extract the error message shown in the following screenshot:
 
 
Figure 12.2: The display of the error message
 
Here is the code for fetching the error message from the private We declare two lists: one for the test result and one for the failed results. A field provides information about and dynamic access to a single field of a class or an interface. The reflected field may be a class (static) field or an instance field. Using this, we will fetch the stepResults We then bypass the security on this field using the setAccessible method passing it the argument ‘true’. We will fetch the step results for the scenario and store it into the local list We will then check for the test results being null or empty. If the test result list is not null or empty, we will use a lambda expression to extract the failed scenarios into the failedResults list. If the failedResults list is not null or empty, we will return the error message from this list. At the end, we will return spaces when the test has passed.
 
private String fetchErrorMsg(Scenario scenario) {
List testResults = null;
List failedResults = null;
try {
Field stepResults =
scenario.getClass().getDeclaredField("stepResults");
//Bypass the security
stepResults.setAccessible(true);
testResults = (List)stepResults.get(scenario);
} catch (NoSuchFieldException|SecurityException |
IllegalArgumentException | IllegalAccessException e) {
// TODO Auto-generated catch block
e.printStackTrace();
}
 
if (testResults != null && !testResults.isEmpty()) {
//pick the results where error message is not null
failedResults = testResults.stream().filter((a) -> {
return a.getErrorMessage() != null;
}).collect(Collectors.toList());
}
 
if (failedResults != null && !failedResults.isEmpty()) {
return failedResults.get(0).getErrorMessage();
}
return "";
}

enshotAs(OutputType.FILE);

This chapter will look at parallel execution on the local and Selenium Grid. Parallel test execution involves running test automation in parallel rather than sequentially. The tester need not execute your tests one by one. Instead of that, the entire batch can be split up into multiple groups, and each group can be executed in parallel. This technique has advantages that can effectively reduce the test execution time and improve your overall software development life cycle.

Let’s start understanding the concepts related to parallel execution along with the Selenium Grid configuration. This is going to be a very important chapter as far as test automation is concerned.

 
13.1 Understand parallel execution
 
Parallel execution helps to reduce the execution time by executing Feature files or scenarios in parallel. This helps in faster turnaround time in case of failures. We can mix and match the execution on different browsers and thus achieve multi browser testing. We can also execute the test cases remotely using Grid as we will see later.
 
If one has enough resources to run all the tests at once, then the duration of the test execution will last only as long as the slowest running test. For example, if you have 100 tests and 100 virtual machines on which to run these tests, then dividing these tests in parallel will allow running 100 tests at once. If your slowest test among the set of 100 takes two minutes to run, then that is how long it will take for the entire test suite to complete the execution.
 
Let’s now understand synchronized methods.

 
13.2 Understanding Synchronized methods
 
Synchronization in Java gives the control to access multiple threads to any resource that is shared.
 
Java synchronization is a good option when it is required that only one thread should be able to access the shared resource. Synchronization is mostly used in programming when we want to prevent the thread interference.
 
There are two types of synchronization in Java:
  
Process synchronization
 
Thread synchronization
 
We will look at only Thread synchronization here. There are two types of synchronizations available in Thread synchronization:
  
Inter thread communication
 
Mutually Exclusive
  
Synchronized method
 
Synchronized block
 
Static synchronization
  
Here, our focus will be on synchronized methods. Synchronized methods enable us to prevent thread interference and prevent memory consistency errors. If an object is visible to more than one thread, all reads or writes to that object’s fields are done through the synchronized method.
 
When the method is static synchronized, the lock is obtained on the class and not on the object. In general, synchronized methods are used to protect access to resources that are accessed concurrently or in parallel. When a resource that is being accessed concurrently belongs to each instance of your class, you use a synchronized instance method; when the resource belongs to all instances (i.e. when it is in a static variable as our ExtentTest and ExtentReports objects as we will see later), then you will use a synchronized static method to access it.
 
We will use static synchronized methods for the creation of Extent reports. We will have two classes, namely, ExtentMgr and Let’s see what these classes will have.

The static synchronized method getReporter() returns the ExtentReports object This method creates the ExtentHtmlReporter object by passing it the filename with the full path as argument. The theme, document title, encoding, and report name are set by invoking the config() method on the ExtentHtmlReporter object. A new ExtentReports object is then created and the ExtentHtmlReporter object is attached to it by invoking the attachReporter(ExtentHtmlReporter) method on the ExtentReports object. Various system information is set on the ExtentReports object by invoking the setSystemInfo(String, The code is shown as follows:
 
public synchronized static ExtentReports getRprtr() {
if (extentReports == null) {
ExtentHtmlReporter htmlReprtr = new
ExtentHtmlReporter(System.getProperty("user.dir")+"/reports
/"+fileName);
htmlReprtr.config().setTheme(Theme.STANDARD);
htmlReprtr.config().setDocumentTitle(fileName);
htmlReprtr.config().setEncoding("utf-8");
htmlReprtr.config().setReportName(fileName);
extentReports = new ExtentReports();
extentReports.attachReporter(htmlReprtr);
extentReports.setSystemInfo("Automation Test Run", "Parallel Execution");
extentReports.setSystemInfo("Organization", "BPB");
extentReports.setSystemInfo("Build no", "BPB-TEST");
}
return extentReports;
}
 
Create a method for capturing screenshots. This method will capture a screenshot as a file object. It creates the screenshot name by appending today’s date and a counter that gets incremented on every call to this method. Finally, the screenshot is copied to the reports folder as follows:
 
public static void captureScreenshot() {
counter = counter + 1;
File scrFile = ((TakesScreenshot)
SingletonDriver.getInstance().getDrvr()).getScreenshotAs(OutputTyp e.FILE);
Date d = new Date();
screenshotName = d.toString().replace(":", "_").replace(" ", "_")
+ "_"+counter+".jpg";
try {
FileUtils.copyFile(scrFile, new
File(System.getProperty("user.dir") + "/reports/" +
screenshotName));
} catch (IOException e) {
// TODO Auto-generated catch block
e.printStackTrace();
}
}

13.4 Creating an Extent Test class
 
Follow the given steps to create the
  
We will first create a ThreadLocal variable for ExtentTest and another variable for ExtentReports and fetch the ExtentReports instance using the getRprtr() method. Both these are static variables as follows:
 
public static ThreadLocal tstReprt = new ThreadLocal();
static ExtentReports extent = ExtentMgr.getRprtr();
 
Fetch the test using the static synchronized method as follows:
 
public static synchronized ExtentTest getTest() {
return tstReprt.get();
}
 
Create log messages for info, passed steps, and failed steps as follows:
 
public static void logInfo(String message) {
tstReprt.get().info(message);
}
 
public static void logPass(String message) {
tstReprt.get().pass(message);
}
 
public static void logFail(String message) {
tstReprt.get().fail(message);
}
 
Create a static method for marking the test case as passed using createLabel(String,ExtentColor) of the MarkupHelper class. Pass the log message and the GREEN enum entry. Get the ThreadLocal variable and pass it the status PASS along with the log message as follows:
 
public static void scenarioPass() {
String passMsg = "Scenario has passed";
Markup m = MarkupHelper.createLabel(passMsg, ExtentColor.GREEN);
tstReprt.get().log(Status.PASS, m);
}

Create a method to start the generation of Extent reports. There are two overloaded methods as follows:
 
public static synchronized ExtentTest startTest(String testName) {
return startTest(testName, "");
}
 
public static synchronized ExtentTest startTest(String testName, String
desc) {
ExtentTest tst = extent.createTest(testName, desc);
tstReprt.set(tst);
return tst;
}
 
This completes the Let’s move on to changes in testng.xml for parallel execution.

 
13.5 Changes to the testng.xml for parallel execution
 
The changes to the testng.xml are simple. We have two tests. One is a positive test and the other is a negative test. In the suite tag, we have mentioned parallel=”tests” so that the tests execute in parallel. We will execute two test runners here. The execution takes place based on the tags in both the test runners:
 
version="1.0" encoding="UTF-8"?>
suite SYSTEM "http://testng.org/testng-1.0.dtd">
name="Suite" parallel="tests">
 
name="Negative Test">
name="testrunner.BPBTR_2"/>
name="Positive Test">
name="testrunner.BPBTR_3"/>
